patient.title: Bevacizumab every 14 days · breast treatment component
patient.context_label: HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer · with paclitaxel
patient.schedule_summary: Bevacizumab infusion on Day 1 of each 14-day cycle with separately prescribed paclitaxel. Continue while the cancer is controlled and treatment is tolerated, with regular review; there is no fixed number of breast-treatment cycles.
patient.purpose: Bevacizumab blocks a signal that helps cancers develop blood vessels. With paclitaxel, it can help delay cancer worsening. The aim in this setting is disease control, with treatment reviewed against benefit and side effects.
patient.indication_text: First-line HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer with paclitaxel. This suite explains the bevacizumab component; paclitaxel and any other treatment need their own plan and assessment.
patient.administration_text: The usual bevacizumab reference dose is 10 mg/kg intravenously every 14 days. The first infusion is over 90 minutes; if tolerated, the second can be over 60 minutes and later infusions over 30 minutes. The team checks the actual prescription, blood pressure, urine and other tests before treatment.
patient.monitoring_summary: Before starting: blood count, kidney and liver tests, urine protein, blood pressure and a heart history/examination. Repeat blood count, kidney/liver tests and urine testing before each cycle; check blood pressure before treatment and after it. Extra checks depend on symptoms and results.

agents.name: Bevacizumab
agents.explanation: Binds VEGF, a signal that promotes blood-vessel growth. Blocking VEGF can reduce the blood supply that supports tumour growth; it also affects normal blood vessels and wound healing.
agents.mechanism: Blocks the VEGF blood-vessel growth signal
visual: Less VEGF signalling supports tumour blood vessels
risks: Raised blood pressure and protein in the urine
Bleeding, blood clots and problems with wound healing
Rare bowel perforation, abnormal internal connections called fistulae, or serious wound infection
Rare severe headache, confusion, seizures or vision changes associated with a brain syndrome
Infusion reactions; fatigue and other effects may be increased by the chemotherapy partner
agents.watch: Report bleeding, severe pain, neurological symptoms or wound problems promptly, and attend blood-pressure and urine checks.

anatomy: Severe headache, confusion, seizures or a change in vision need urgent help.
Attend blood-pressure checks; chest pain, breathlessness or a swollen painful leg need urgent help.
Urine checks look for protein. Report new swelling, foamy urine or reduced urine.
Sudden severe abdominal pain needs urgent assessment.
Report bleeding or wounds that are painful, red, spreading or slow to heal.
A new swollen painful leg or sudden breathlessness needs urgent help.
patient.anatomy_note: Symptoms are prompts to contact the team, not a diagnosis. Paclitaxel has additional effects covered in its own guide.

patient.urgent_extra: Seek urgent help for sudden severe abdominal pain, significant bleeding or coughing blood, chest pain, breathlessness, a swollen painful leg, a severe headache, confusion, seizures, a change in vision, or a rapidly painful/red spreading wound. Follow the chemotherapy emergency plan for fever or feeling acutely unwell.

sections.title: Infusion visits
sections.text: The usual bevacizumab reference dose is 10 mg/kg intravenously every 14 days. The first infusion is over 90 minutes; if tolerated, the second can be over 60 minutes and later infusions over 30 minutes. The team checks the actual prescription, blood pressure, urine and other tests before treatment.

sections.title: Checks and samples
sections.text: Allow time for blood tests, a urine sample and blood-pressure checks. A 24-hour urine collection may be needed between visits; confirm when the team needs the result.

sections.title: Partner treatment
sections.text: Paclitaxel may be given on different days from bevacizumab. Bring both treatment plans; a change to one medicine does not automatically change the other.

sections.title: Access and procedures
sections.text: Bevacizumab needs an intravenous cannula or existing suitable central line; the team decides access. Tell the team about surgery, dental work or wounds before booking procedures.

sections.title: Support contacts
sections.text: Keep the daytime and out-of-hours oncology numbers available. If a visit or test is missed, contact the team for a revised plan rather than rearranging treatment yourself.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: Adding bevacizumab to paclitaxel can delay worsening of metastatic breast cancer for some people.
evidence.population: First-line HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer with paclitaxel
evidence.interpretation: The supporting study showed a delay in cancer worsening; a longer overall survival was not established. The team weighs this against side effects and treatment burden.
evidence.limitations: The supporting paclitaxel trial used bevacizumab every two weeks. That matches this bevacizumab schedule. Discuss the expected benefit and alternatives for your own situation.

patient.teachback: Which days have bevacizumab and paclitaxel, when are blood-pressure and urine checks, which symptoms need urgent help, and who must know about surgery or a wound?
patient.consent_support: Discuss disease-control goals and alternatives, the lack of established overall-survival improvement in the supporting paclitaxel study, blood-pressure and proteinuria monitoring, bleeding and clotting, bowel perforation/fistula, wound healing, infusion reactions, reproductive precautions and the additional risks of paclitaxel.

support.title: Blood pressure and urine
support.text: Take prescribed blood-pressure medicines as agreed and attend urine checks. If a 24-hour collection is requested, confirm how to collect and return it before the next treatment.

support.title: Surgery, wounds and teeth
support.text: Tell the team about planned operations, dental procedures and any wound that is not healing. Bevacizumab can require a treatment break around procedures; the team sets the timing.

support.title: Separate chemotherapy support
support.text: Bevacizumab itself usually needs no routine anti-sickness premedication. Paclitaxel has separate allergy-prevention, anti-sickness and symptom plans; keep both plans and the emergency contact details.

support.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
support.text: Discuss fertility and effective contraception before treatment and continue contraception during treatment and for at least six months after the last bevacizumab dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment or for at least six months after the final dose. The partner treatment may require additional precautions.

questions.q: Is this a stand-alone breast treatment?
questions.a: This breast regimen uses bevacizumab with paclitaxel. Any change to the chemotherapy partner or a continuation plan must be agreed with your oncologist.

questions.q: How long will I have treatment?
questions.a: There is no fixed number of breast-treatment cycles. Your team reviews cancer control, side effects and your preferences and agrees when to continue, pause or change.

questions.q: What happens if urine protein or blood pressure rises?
questions.a: The team may repeat tests, treat blood pressure or pause bevacizumab. Severe problems may mean stopping it. Do not restart after a pause without an agreed plan.

questions.q: What if I need an operation or dental work?
questions.a: Tell the oncology team before the procedure. Bevacizumab can slow healing, and the team must coordinate any treatment break and check healing before restarting.

chronology_notes.title: Different schedules
chronology_notes.text: Bevacizumab repeats every 14 days; the chemotherapy partner can follow a different cycle. Check both plans at every change.

chronology_notes.title: Treatment pauses
chronology_notes.text: A pause for surgery, high blood pressure, proteinuria or another effect needs a new team plan; a calendar alone cannot determine a safe restart.

rationale.line: First-line metastatic breast treatment with paclitaxel; no adjuvant indication or unrestricted breast monotherapy implied.
factors: Confirm HER2-negative metastatic disease, prior therapy, ECOG, comorbidity, alternatives and patient priorities.
Balance delay in progression against bleeding, hypertension, proteinuria, thrombotic, wound and bowel risks.
Confirm the intended bevacizumab interval, companion schedule and local approval/reimbursement.
alternatives: Other systemic and supportive approaches depend on receptor status, biomarkers, previous therapy, pace of disease and patient preference; no cross-trial ranking is supplied.
limitations: This is a shared bevacizumab component protocol; companion chemotherapy or other SACT is not assessed by these rules.

NCCP 00212 v7 states that no bevacizumab dose adjustment is expected for renal impairment, hepatic impairment or haemodialysis. Review severity, clinical suitability and partner treatment; this does not override proteinuria or other stop/hold rules.

NCCP BP notation >150/100 and >200/110 does not explicitly state how to combine isolated systolic and diastolic abnormalities. A clinician confirms uncontrolled/severe BP; no invented binary calculation is used.
Grade 3 hypertension requires persistence before source discontinuation applies. A new grade 3 event alone is not encoded as a permanent-stop criterion.
NCCP grades in the bevacizumab toxicity table do not identify a CTCAE edition. Existing interface CTCAE v5 descriptions are orientation aids; source grading must be confirmed.
Trial averages do not predict individual benefit. E2100 findings must not be applied to adjuvant disease, other tumour types or every chemotherapy partner.
Normal proteinuria results do not clear unassessed blood pressure, surgical, bleeding or partner-treatment domains.

EMA E2100 Table 10 and the original journal analysis use different assessment/data-cut presentations. This record uses only the EMA Table 10 investigator analysis and its stated overall-survival analysis; no estimates are mixed.

eligibility_orientation: Adult, ECOG 0–2 and adequate organ function; confirm disease, line, biomarker and partner.
important_cautions: Review prior anthracycline/chest-wall radiotherapy, pelvic radiotherapy, cardiovascular and renal disease, bleeding/clotting history, major/minor procedures and fistula/perforation risk.
Recent pulmonary haemorrhage/haemoptysis >2.5 mL red blood: EMA says do not treat.
Pregnancy is excluded; no breastfeeding during treatment or six months afterwards. Effective contraception during and six months after bevacizumab; reconcile the partner plan.

baseline: Confirm adult first-line HER2-negative metastatic breast disease and paclitaxel plan; review ECOG 0–2 eligibility.
FBC, renal and liver profile; urine protein; blood pressure.
Cardiac history and examination; consider ECHO after prior anthracycline or chest-wall radiotherapy. INR if indicated.
Review surgery/wound healing, bleeding and thromboembolic risks, pelvic radiotherapy and perforation/fistula risks; medicines and reproductive precautions.
before_each_cycle: FBC, renal/liver profile, urinalysis, BP and symptom/medicine/wound review.
BP before each cycle and after treatment; partner therapy must also be assessed.
ongoing: BP more frequently if hypertension develops/worsens.
Urine dipstick 2+/3+ or spot urine ≥1 g/L: 24-hour urine collection within 3 days before next dose. Dipstick 4+: hold pending quantification.
24-hour urine >2 to 4 g: hold, recheck every two weeks, resume ≤2 g/24 h after review; >4 g: discontinue.
Warfarin INR weekly until stable then before each cycle.
Consider ECHO at baseline for prior anthracycline/chest-wall radiotherapy; repeat testing is individual, not a copied trastuzumab schedule.
Cancer monitoring follows the individual consultant treatment plan.
access: IV infusion in 100 mL sodium chloride 0.9%; no IV bolus/push.
90-minute first infusion; if tolerated, 60-minute second and then 30-minute later infusions. A rapid/off-label infusion requires separate local policy, consent and governance.

evidence.population: Previously untreated locally recurrent/metastatic breast cancer; trial majority HER2-negative (90%); NCCP breast indication is HER2-negative metastatic disease.
evidence.comparison: Bevacizumab 10 mg/kg every two weeks + weekly paclitaxel versus weekly paclitaxel alone.
evidence.applicability: Direct bevacizumab dose/interval and partner evidence for 00212; trial treatment and current NCCP eligibility still require reconciliation.
evidence.qualitative_result: Improved progression-free survival with the combination; no statistically significant overall-survival improvement established.

endpoints.result_text: Median 11.4 months with bevacizumab/paclitaxel versus 5.8 months with paclitaxel; HR 0.421 (95% CI 0.343–0.516), p<0.0001.
endpoints.interpretation: EMA investigator primary analysis for 10 mg/kg every two weeks plus paclitaxel. Independent-review results are a separate dataset and are not mixed here.

support.text: Take prescribed blood-pressure medicines as agreed and attend urine checks. If a 24-hour collection is requested, confirm how to collect and return it before the next treatment.

support.title: Surgery, wounds and teeth
support.text: Tell the team about planned operations, dental procedures and any wound that is not healing. Bevacizumab can require a treatment break around procedures; the team sets the timing.

support.title: Separate chemotherapy support
support.text: Bevacizumab itself usually needs no routine anti-sickness premedication. Paclitaxel has separate allergy-prevention, anti-sickness and symptom plans; keep both plans and the emergency contact details.

support.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
support.text: Discuss fertility and effective contraception before treatment and continue contraception during treatment and for at least six months after the last bevacizumab dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment or for at least six months after the final dose. The partner treatment may require additional precautions.

questions.q: Is this a stand-alone breast treatment?
questions.a: This breast regimen uses bevacizumab with paclitaxel. Any change to the chemotherapy partner or a continuation plan must be agreed with your oncologist.

questions.q: How long will I have treatment?
questions.a: There is no fixed number of breast-treatment cycles. Your team reviews cancer control, side effects and your preferences and agrees when to continue, pause or change.

questions.q: What happens if urine protein or blood pressure rises?
questions.a: The team may repeat tests, treat blood pressure or pause bevacizumab. Severe problems may mean stopping it. Do not restart after a pause without an agreed plan.

questions.q: What if I need an operation or dental work?
questions.a: Tell the oncology team before the procedure. Bevacizumab can slow healing, and the team must coordinate any treatment break and check healing before restarting.

chronology_notes.text: A pause for surgery, high blood pressure, proteinuria or another effect needs a new team plan; a calendar alone cannot determine a safe restart.

chapters.title: Treatment and its aim
chapters.intro: Bevacizumab blocks a signal that helps cancers develop blood vessels. With paclitaxel, it can help delay cancer worsening. The aim in this setting is disease control, with treatment reviewed against benefit and side effects.

items.title: Who this guide covers
items.text: First-line HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer with paclitaxel. This suite explains the bevacizumab component; paclitaxel and any other treatment need their own plan and assessment.

items.title: Infusion schedule
items.text: The usual bevacizumab reference dose is 15 mg/kg intravenously every 21 days. The first infusion is over 90 minutes; if tolerated, the second can be over 60 minutes and later infusions over 30 minutes. The team checks the actual prescription, blood pressure, urine and other tests before treatment.

items.title: Evidence and personal choice
items.text: The supporting study showed a delay in cancer worsening; a longer overall survival was not established. The team weighs this against side effects and treatment burden. The supporting paclitaxel trial used bevacizumab every two weeks. It did not directly test this every-three-week bevacizumab schedule. Discuss the expected benefit and alternatives for your own situation.

chapters.title: Tests and review
chapters.intro: Before starting: blood count, kidney and liver tests, urine protein, blood pressure and a heart history/examination. Repeat blood count, kidney/liver tests and urine testing before each cycle; check blood pressure before treatment and after it. Extra checks depend on symptoms and results.

items.title: Urine results
items.text: Protein in the urine can require a 24-hour collection and additional checks. Your team explains how and when to collect it, and reviews whether treatment can continue.

items.title: Heart and blood-thinning medicines
items.text: An ultrasound of the heart may be considered if you have had certain earlier chemotherapy or chest-wall radiotherapy. If you take warfarin, INR tests are usually weekly until stable and then before each cycle; follow your individual plan.

items.title: Cancer response
items.text: Scans and cancer-response checks follow the individual consultant plan. This guide does not promise a fixed scan or repeat heart-ultrasound schedule.

chapters.title: Support and urgent symptoms
chapters.intro: Seek urgent help for sudden severe abdominal pain, significant bleeding or coughing blood, chest pain, breathlessness, a swollen painful leg, a severe headache, confusion, seizures, a change in vision, or a rapidly painful/red spreading wound. Follow the chemotherapy emergency plan for fever or feeling acutely unwell.

patient.title: Everolimus + exemestane
patient.context_label: Postmenopausal HR-positive / HER2-negative advanced breast cancer
patient.schedule_summary: Usual starting doses are everolimus 10 mg once daily and exemestane 25 mg once daily; use the doses on your prescription. Both tablets are taken every day continuously. There is no planned rest week. Review benefit and tolerability over time; there is no fixed adjuvant completion date.
patient.purpose: Exemestane lowers oestrogen production while everolimus blocks an intracellular growth pathway that can contribute to endocrine resistance. The aim in this setting is to control cancer and delay progression.
patient.indication_text: Postmenopausal HR-positive/HER2-negative advanced disease after recurrence/progression following an NSAI, without symptomatic visceral disease. The intended endocrine partner is exemestane; do not automatically substitute another endocrine drug.
patient.administration_text: Take everolimus at the same time daily, consistently with food or consistently without food. Take exemestane after a meal. Swallow tablets whole with water; do not crush or chew. If a dose is missed, take the next scheduled dose without adding an extra dose.
patient.monitoring_summary: FBC, renal and liver profile; blood urea nitrogen and urinary protein. Blood glucose, total cholesterol and triglycerides; optimise pre-existing metabolic abnormalities. Review lung symptoms, infection, mouth health, all medicines, planned surgery/radiotherapy and exemestane bone risk. FBC, renal/liver profile, total cholesterol and triglycerides every four weeks or as clinically indicated. Fasting glucose as clinically indicated, with closer surveillance for diabetes or increased risk. At reviews assess mouth ulcers, intake, infection, cough/breathlessness, oedema, skin/bowel symptoms and adherence. Disease assessment and imaging follow the consultant plan; new symptoms can bring review forward.
patient.review_status: Source reconciled; independent clinical, pharmacy and patient/PPI review pending

agents.name: Everolimus
agents.explanation: Everolimus binds the intracellular protein FKBP12; this complex inhibits mTORC1, affecting protein synthesis and growth signalling. This pathway can support endocrine resistance, which explains pairing it with an oestrogen-lowering medicine. The same pathway operates in normal tissues, contributing to mouth ulcers, infection risk and metabolic changes.
agents.watch: Report new mouth soreness, cough/breathlessness, fever/infection symptoms, diarrhoea or excessive thirst promptly. A new cough must not simply be labelled drug pneumonitis without checking other causes.
risks: Impaired wound healing and radiation-related toxicity

agents.name: Exemestane
agents.mechanism: Irreversibly inhibits aromatase and lowers oestrogen production
agents.explanation: After menopause, aromatase in tissues converts androgen precursors into oestrogen. Exemestane is an irreversible aromatase inhibitor that reduces this supply to hormone-sensitive cancer cells. It does not directly switch off functioning ovaries; the menopausal indication must be confirmed.
agents.watch: Tell the team if joint pain, hot flushes, vaginal dryness or sleep disturbance affects daily life. Bone thinning can be silent, so keep the agreed bone-health reviews.

sections.title: Before starting
sections.text: Confirm the exact medicine, strength, endocrine partner, baseline tests and first review appointments. Ask who arranges tests and who reviews the results.

sections.title: Taking treatment
sections.text: Take everolimus at the same time daily, consistently with food or consistently without food. Take exemestane after a meal. Swallow tablets whole with water; do not crush or chew. If a dose is missed, take the next scheduled dose without adding an extra dose.

sections.title: Treatment duration
sections.text: Continue while beneficial and tolerated; review each medicine separately if everolimus is held.

sections.title: Supply and appointments
sections.text: Request the next supply before tablets run out. Blood tests and any ECG or injections need their own appointments. This oral treatment does not itself require a central line or infusion pump.

sections.title: If treatment is held
sections.text: Ask which medicine is held, whether the endocrine partner continues, what needs to recover, when the next review is due and who will authorise restart.

sections.title: Support between appointments
sections.text: Keep the oncology contact details and prescribed symptom medicines accessible. New severe symptoms need prompt assessment rather than waiting for the next blood test.

evidence.title: BOLERO-2
evidence.intro: Studies describe groups. Ask how closely the treatment and study population match your situation.
evidence.population: Postmenopausal HR-positive/HER2-negative advanced breast cancer progressing during or after a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor; 724 randomized patients.
evidence.interpretation: Adding everolimus to exemestane delayed cancer growth compared with exemestane alone in the study. The trial did not show a clear improvement in how long people lived overall. This older study cannot give a precise estimate for someone previously treated with modern CDK4/6 combinations.
evidence.limitations: Your team can discuss the strength and limitations of the evidence alongside treatment risks and alternatives.

patient.teachback: Which medicine is taken when, which test is due next, who reviews it, and which symptoms mean you should call today?
patient.consent_support: Discuss the treatment aim, alternatives, benefit and uncertainty, important medicine-specific risks, reproductive precautions, symptom support and planned duration. Confirm the endocrine partner and any ovarian-suppression plan. The timeline does not authorise a restart or certify clinical review.

support.title: Nausea support
support.text: Everolimus is oral minimal–low emetic risk. No routine infusion premedication is needed; agree individual rescue treatment and local oral-SACT advice.

support.title: Mouth care from the start
support.text: Agree non-alcoholic mouth care and whether a prescribed alcohol-free corticosteroid mouthwash is appropriate during the first eight weeks. Report mouth ulcers early and check for thrush rather than adding an antifungal automatically.

support.title: Lungs and infection
support.text: New cough, breathlessness or fever needs prompt review. If systemic steroids or other immunosuppression are used, the team considers PJP prevention according to risk.

support.title: Metabolic and bone health
support.text: Keep glucose, cholesterol, kidney and liver checks. Discuss diabetes/lipid care, exemestane bone risk, exercise, diet and any indicated bone-protection treatment.

support.title: Surgery, radiotherapy and other medicines
support.text: Tell both oncology and procedure teams about everolimus before surgery or radiotherapy. Check all new medicines and supplements; avoid grapefruit and St John’s wort.

items.text: Usual starting doses are everolimus 10 mg once daily and exemestane 25 mg once daily; use the doses on your prescription. Both tablets are taken every day continuously. There is no planned rest week. Review benefit and tolerability over time; there is no fixed adjuvant completion date. items.title: Before the first dose
items.text: FBC, renal and liver profile; blood urea nitrogen and urinary protein. Blood glucose, total cholesterol and triglycerides; optimise pre-existing metabolic abnormalities. Review lung symptoms, infection, mouth health, all medicines, planned surgery/radiotherapy and exemestane bone risk.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: FBC, renal/liver profile, total cholesterol and triglycerides every four weeks or as clinically indicated. Fasting glucose as clinically indicated, with closer surveillance for diabetes or increased risk. At reviews assess mouth ulcers, intake, infection, cough/breathlessness, oedema, skin/bowel symptoms and adherence. Disease assessment and imaging follow the consultant plan; new symptoms can bring review forward.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: Supportive medicines and the endocrine partner have their own plan.

items.title: Nausea support
items.text: Everolimus is oral minimal–low emetic risk. No routine infusion premedication is needed; agree individual rescue treatment and local oral-SACT advice.

items.title: Mouth care from the start
items.text: Agree non-alcoholic mouth care and whether a prescribed alcohol-free corticosteroid mouthwash is appropriate during the first eight weeks. Report mouth ulcers early and check for thrush rather than adding an antifungal automatically.

items.title: Lungs and infection
items.text: New cough, breathlessness or fever needs prompt review. If systemic steroids or other immunosuppression are used, the team considers PJP prevention according to risk.

items.title: Metabolic and bone health
items.text: Keep glucose, cholesterol, kidney and liver checks. Discuss diabetes/lipid care, exemestane bone risk, exercise, diet and any indicated bone-protection treatment.

items.title: Surgery, radiotherapy and other medicines
items.text: Tell both oncology and procedure teams about everolimus before surgery or radiotherapy. Check all new medicines and supplements; avoid grapefruit and St John’s wort.

chapters.title: What the studies tell us
chapters.intro: Adding everolimus to exemestane delayed cancer growth compared with exemestane alone in the study. The trial did not show a clear improvement in how long people lived overall. This older study cannot give a precise estimate for someone previously treated with modern CDK4/6 combinations.

items.title: How to interpret this
items.text: Study results describe groups with defined treatment and eligibility. Ask about your own likely benefits, important harms, alternatives and remaining uncertainty.

chapters.title: When the plan changes
chapters.intro: Continue while beneficial and tolerated; review each medicine separately if everolimus is held.

items.title: Continue, hold or stop
items.text: The team confirms the plan for each medicine and the next review. Do not restart a clinically held treatment from this educational timeline.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates?
questions.a: No. This map shows general timing without personal information. Your hospital arranges actual appointments; ask who books each test and who reviews its result.

questions.q: What if a dose is missed or treatment is held?
questions.a: Take everolimus at the same time daily, consistently with food or consistently without food. Take exemestane after a meal. Swallow tablets whole with water; do not crush or chew. If a dose is missed, take the next scheduled dose without adding an extra dose. A hold may affect one medicine rather than the whole combination; confirm each component.

rationale.summary: Exemestane lowers oestrogen production while everolimus blocks an intracellular growth pathway that can contribute to endocrine resistance. The aim in this setting is to control cancer and delay progression.
rationale.setting: Postmenopausal HR-positive / HER2-negative advanced breast cancer
rationale.line: Postmenopausal HR-positive/HER2-negative advanced disease after recurrence/progression following an NSAI, without symptomatic visceral disease. The intended endocrine partner is exemestane; do not automatically substitute another endocrine drug.

alternatives: Discuss endocrine therapy alone, another indication-appropriate endocrine/targeted approach, or other systemic treatment according to disease setting, previous treatment, risk, tolerability and patient priorities. No direct superiority ranking is implied.
limitations: NCCP and product information have differing renal/hepatic wording in some situations; retain the existing specialist-review pathways.
Everolimus can cause pneumonitis, immunosuppression, metabolic/renal toxicity and impaired wound healing or radiation toxicity.
Pre-CDK4/6 trial; it does not quantify benefit after current CDK4/6 combinations.
Do not substitute adjuvant endpoints or an individual prognosis for these advanced-disease results.

clinical.component_rationale: Everolimus: Everolimus binds the intracellular protein FKBP12; this complex inhibits mTORC1, affecting protein synthesis and growth signalling. This pathway can support endocrine resistance, which explains pairing it with an oestrogen-lowering medicine. The same pathway operates in normal tissues, contributing to mouth ulcers, infection risk and metabolic changes. Exemestane: After menopause, aromatase in tissues converts androgen precursors into oestrogen. Exemestane is an irreversible aromatase inhibitor that reduces this supply to hormone-sensitive cancer cells. It does not directly switch off functioning ovaries; the menopausal indication must be confirmed.

patient.title: Palbociclib with endocrine therapy
patient.context_label: HR-positive, HER2-negative locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer
patient.schedule_label: Oral treatment with a planned rest week
patient.schedule_summary: The usual palbociclib starting dose is 125 mg once daily; a lower dose may be prescribed. Palbociclib is taken once daily on Days 1–21, then paused on Days 22–28 of each 28-day cycle. The aromatase inhibitor continues daily, or fulvestrant follows its injection schedule. Ovarian suppression has its own plan when required.
patient.purpose: Palbociclib slows cell-cycle progression while the hormone partner reduces oestrogen signalling. The aim in this advanced-disease pathway is cancer control, with treatment and response reviewed over time.
patient.indication_text: HR-positive/HER2-negative locally advanced/metastatic disease with an AI, or with fulvestrant after previous endocrine therapy as defined in NCCP. Pre/perimenopausal endocrine treatment requires ovarian suppression; the exact partner and its risks must be confirmed.
patient.administration_text: Check whether the pharmacy supplied capsules or tablets: capsules are taken with food; tablets can be taken with or without food. Swallow whole at a consistent time. Avoid grapefruit. If you miss or vomit a dose, do not take an extra dose; take the next scheduled dose. Do not restart after a clinical hold until the treating team confirms.
patient.monitoring_summary: FBC, renal and liver profile. Confirm receptor status, exact endocrine partner, previous endocrine therapy, menopause/ovarian suppression, pregnancy precautions and interacting medicines. FBC on Day 1 and Day 15 of cycles 1–2; Day 1 from cycle 3 and extra checks as indicated. Only after at most grade 1–2 neutropenia throughout the first six cycles may FBC monitoring reduce to every three months, before the start of a cycle and as indicated. Renal and liver profile before each cycle; review fever/infection, mouth/bowel symptoms, fatigue, pulmonary symptoms and adherence. No routine palbociclib-specific Day-14 ECG or echo timetable; investigate when clinically indicated.
patient.review_status: Source reconciled; independent clinical, pharmacy and patient/PPI review pending

agents.name: Palbociclib
agents.mechanism: Blocks cell-cycle signals that help cancer cells divide
agents.explanation: Hormone signalling can activate cyclin-D/CDK4/6. Palbociclib blocks this control point, helping keep susceptible cells from progressing through the cell cycle. Combining it with endocrine therapy acts on both the hormonal signal and downstream cell division.
agents.watch: The key early issue is a falling white-cell count, which may cause no symptoms. Keep blood-test appointments and report infection symptoms or new cough/breathlessness promptly.
risks: Rare but serious interstitial lung disease / pneumonitis

agents.name: Your endocrine partner
agents.type: Either an aromatase inhibitor or fulvestrant
agents.mechanism: Reduces oestrogen signalling to hormone-sensitive cells
visual: AI lowers oestrogen; fulvestrant targets its receptor
agents.explanation: An aromatase inhibitor lowers oestrogen production; fulvestrant acts at the oestrogen receptor. These are alternative partners here, not an instruction to take both. The partner’s dose, monitoring and injection or tablet schedule must be confirmed.
agents.watch: Discuss joint/hot-flush and bone symptoms with an AI, or injection-site/bleeding symptoms with fulvestrant. Pre/perimenopausal women require ovarian suppression in the prescribed combination.
risks: Hot flushes and other hormone-related symptoms
AI: joint symptoms and bone loss
Partner-specific liver, interaction and pregnancy considerations

sections.title: Before starting
sections.text: Confirm the exact medicine, strength, endocrine partner, baseline tests and first review appointments. Ask who arranges tests and who reviews the results.

sections.title: Taking treatment
sections.text: Check whether the pharmacy supplied capsules or tablets: capsules are taken with food; tablets can be taken with or without food. Swallow whole at a consistent time. Avoid grapefruit. If you miss or vomit a dose, do not take an extra dose; take the next scheduled dose. Do not restart after a clinical hold until the treating team confirms.

sections.title: Your endocrine partner has a separate timetable
sections.text: An aromatase inhibitor is normally taken daily through the targeted-medicine rest week. If fulvestrant is the chosen partner, the usual schedule is 500 mg by intramuscular injection on Days 1, 15 and 29, then once monthly; confirm the prescribed dose and appointment dates. Any ovarian-suppression injections have their own schedule.

sections.title: Treatment duration
sections.text: Repeat while beneficial and tolerated. The planned week off concerns palbociclib, not automatically the endocrine partner.

sections.title: Supply and appointments
sections.text: Request the next supply before tablets run out. Blood tests and any ECG or injections need their own appointments. This oral treatment does not itself require a central line or infusion pump.

sections.title: If treatment is held
sections.text: Ask which medicine is held, whether the endocrine partner continues, what needs to recover, when the next review is due and who will authorise restart.

sections.title: Support between appointments
sections.text: Keep the oncology contact details and prescribed symptom medicines accessible. New severe symptoms need prompt assessment rather than waiting for the next blood test.

evidence.title: PALOMA-2 and PALOMA-3: keep endocrine partner and analysis separate
evidence.intro: Studies describe groups. Ask how closely the treatment and study population match your situation.
evidence.population: PALOMA-2: 666 postmenopausal women with ER-positive/HER2-negative advanced disease and no previous systemic therapy for advanced disease. PALOMA-3: 521 women with progression or relapse during prior endocrine therapy.
evidence.interpretation: Palbociclib with hormone therapy can delay cancer growth. Studies used different hormone partners and different prior-treatment groups. The final overall trial results did not establish a clear survival improvement with palbociclib; later exploratory follow-up needs to be interpreted separately.
evidence.limitations: Your team can discuss the strength and limitations of the evidence alongside treatment risks and alternatives.

patient.teachback: Which medicine is taken when, which test is due next, who reviews it, and which symptoms mean you should call today?
patient.consent_support: Discuss the treatment aim, alternatives, benefit and uncertainty, important medicine-specific risks, reproductive precautions, symptom support and planned duration. Confirm the endocrine partner and any ovarian-suppression plan. The timeline does not authorise a restart or certify clinical review.

support.title: Nausea support
support.text: Palbociclib is oral minimal–low emetic risk. Premedication is not usually required; agree rescue treatment if symptoms occur.

support.title: Blood counts and infection
support.text: Attend early and pre-cycle blood tests. Dose holds and reductions are clinician decisions. Growth-factor injections are not a routine automatic prescription for every patient.

support.title: Endocrine-partner support
support.text: Agree help for hot flushes, joints, vaginal or sexual symptoms, sleep and bone health. Fulvestrant injection discomfort and any ovarian-suppression injections have separate support plans.

support.title: Formulation and interactions
support.text: Check whether the pack contains capsules or tablets and follow the food instructions for that product. Check new medicines, supplements and grapefruit interactions.

support.title: Symptoms between visits
support.text: Report mouth ulcers, persistent bowel symptoms, worsening fatigue, fever or new breathing symptoms promptly.

timeline.label: Endocrine partner
timeline.text: AI every day OR fulvestrant at its scheduled injection visits

timeline.text: May occur without symptoms. FBC Day 1 and Day 15 of first 2 cycles; extra tests if low.

patient.timeline_note: Treatment days are specified by the regimen. Symptom timing varies; the full-cycle symptom bands show that an effect can occur at any point, not a measured probability or severity.

chronology_notes.title: Treatment and rest
chronology_notes.text: Take palbociclib for 21 days, then have 7 days without palbociclib. The aromatase-inhibitor tablet continues every day, or fulvestrant injections follow their separate schedule. The week off applies to palbociclib, not automatically to the hormone treatment.

chronology_notes.title: Tests and appointments
chronology_notes.text: Use the monitoring table for baseline and later checks. A rest week does not remove infection or other risks.

patient.safety_note: Contact the treatment team promptly if you feel feverish or unwell, have shaking chills or infection symptoms, or develop new cough or breathlessness. Follow the local emergency temperature instructions; do not wait for a planned blood test or for the 38.5°C value used in one clinician dose-adjustment table. chapters.title: Your treatment aim
chapters.intro: Palbociclib slows cell-cycle progression while the hormone partner reduces oestrogen signalling. The aim in this advanced-disease pathway is cancer control, with treatment and response reviewed over time.

items.title: Who this treatment is for
items.text: HR-positive/HER2-negative locally advanced/metastatic disease with an AI, or with fulvestrant after previous endocrine therapy as defined in NCCP. Pre/perimenopausal endocrine treatment requires ovarian suppression; the exact partner and its risks must be confirmed.

items.title: Schedule and duration
items.text: The usual palbociclib starting dose is 125 mg once daily; a lower dose may be prescribed. Palbociclib is taken once daily on Days 1–21, then paused on Days 22–28 of each 28-day cycle. The aromatase inhibitor continues daily, or fulvestrant follows its injection schedule. Ovarian suppression has its own plan when required. Repeat while beneficial and tolerated. The planned week off concerns palbociclib, not automatically the endocrine partner.

items.title: Before the first dose
items.text: FBC, renal and liver profile. Confirm receptor status, exact endocrine partner, previous endocrine therapy, menopause/ovarian suppression, pregnancy precautions and interacting medicines.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: FBC on Day 1 and Day 15 of cycles 1–2; Day 1 from cycle 3 and extra checks as indicated. Only after at most grade 1–2 neutropenia throughout the first six cycles may FBC monitoring reduce to every three months, before the start of a cycle and as indicated. Renal and liver profile before each cycle; review fever/infection, mouth/bowel symptoms, fatigue, pulmonary symptoms and adherence. No routine palbociclib-specific Day-14 ECG or echo timetable; investigate when clinically indicated.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: Supportive medicines and the endocrine partner have their own plan.

items.title: Nausea support
items.text: Palbociclib is oral minimal–low emetic risk. Premedication is not usually required; agree rescue treatment if symptoms occur.

items.title: Blood counts and infection
items.text: Attend early and pre-cycle blood tests. Dose holds and reductions are clinician decisions. Growth-factor injections are not a routine automatic prescription for every patient.

items.title: Endocrine-partner support
items.text: Agree help for hot flushes, joints, vaginal or sexual symptoms, sleep and bone health. Fulvestrant injection discomfort and any ovarian-suppression injections have separate support plans.

items.title: Formulation and interactions
items.text: Check whether the pack contains capsules or tablets and follow the food instructions for that product. Check new medicines, supplements and grapefruit interactions.

items.title: Symptoms between visits
items.text: Report mouth ulcers, persistent bowel symptoms, worsening fatigue, fever or new breathing symptoms promptly.

chapters.title: What the studies tell us
chapters.intro: Palbociclib with hormone therapy can delay cancer growth. Studies used different hormone partners and different prior-treatment groups. The final overall trial results did not establish a clear survival improvement with palbociclib; later exploratory follow-up needs to be interpreted separately.

items.title: How to interpret this
items.text: Study results describe groups with defined treatment and eligibility. Ask about your own likely benefits, important harms, alternatives and remaining uncertainty.

chapters.title: When the plan changes
chapters.intro: Repeat while beneficial and tolerated. The planned week off concerns palbociclib, not automatically the endocrine partner.

clinical.component_rationale: Palbociclib: Hormone signalling can activate cyclin-D/CDK4/6. Palbociclib blocks this control point, helping keep susceptible cells from progressing through the cell cycle. Combining it with endocrine therapy acts on both the hormonal signal and downstream cell division. Your endocrine partner: An aromatase inhibitor lowers oestrogen production; fulvestrant acts at the oestrogen receptor. These are alternative partners here, not an instruction to take both. The partner’s dose, monitoring and injection or tablet schedule must be confirmed.

evidence.trial: PALOMA-2 and PALOMA-3: keep endocrine partner and analysis separate
evidence.population: PALOMA-2: 666 postmenopausal women with ER-positive/HER2-negative advanced disease and no previous systemic therapy for advanced disease. PALOMA-3: 521 women with progression or relapse during prior endocrine therapy.
evidence.comparison: PALOMA-2: palbociclib plus letrozole versus placebo plus letrozole. PALOMA-3: palbociclib plus fulvestrant versus placebo plus fulvestrant.
evidence.applicability: PALOMA-2 supports the first-line AI context; PALOMA-3 supports the prior-endocrine/fulvestrant context. Neither is an adjuvant regimen.
evidence.qualitative_result: Palbociclib delayed progression. Final protocol-specified OS was not significantly improved in the overall population of either trial; later PALOMA-3 exploratory follow-up must retain its exploratory label.

agents.name: Ribociclib
agents.explanation: Ribociclib blocks CDK4 and CDK6, proteins that help cells move through the cycle of division. Endocrine therapy reduces the hormone signal that can drive HR-positive breast cancer.

support.title: Electrolytes and heart rhythm
support.text: Correct abnormal potassium, calcium, magnesium and phosphate as directed. Attend the baseline and cycle 1 Day-14 ECG; fainting or palpitations need urgent advice.

questions.q: How long does treatment last?
questions.a: The usual metastatic starting dose is ribociclib 600 mg once daily on Days 1–21 followed by Days 22–28 off. Continue the prescribed AI daily or fulvestrant on its own injection schedule; add ovarian suppression when indicated. Continue while beneficial and tolerated. There is no fixed three-year stop in this metastatic regimen; the team reviews response, side effects and the next treatment decision.

questions.q: Which checks happen before and during treatment?
questions.a: FBC, renal and liver profile, potassium, calcium, magnesium and phosphorus. ECG before initiation; QTcF must be below 450 ms. Correct electrolyte abnormalities and review QT/CYP3A interactions. Confirm endocrine partner, menopause/ovarian suppression, prior treatment and the NCCP indication/eligibility discrepancy. FBC, renal and liver profile every two weeks for cycles 1–2, then before cycles 3–6, then as clinically indicated. Electrolytes before each of the first six cycles, then as clinically indicated; correct abnormalities. Repeat ECG around Day 14 of cycle 1, then as clinically indicated. Increase liver monitoring for grade 2 or worse abnormalities. Review fever, jaundice, palpitations/fainting, pulmonary and severe skin symptoms; response imaging follows the advanced-disease plan.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates?
questions.a: No. This map shows general timing without personal information. Your hospital arranges actual appointments; ask who books each test and who reviews its result.

questions.q: What if a dose is missed or treatment is held?
questions.a: Take ribociclib once daily with or without food; swallow whole. Avoid grapefruit. If a dose is missed or vomited, do not take an extra dose; take the next scheduled dose. Confirm any clinical hold and restart with the team. The endocrine partner follows a separate prescription. A hold may affect one medicine rather than the whole combination; confirm each component.

questions.q: What does the evidence mean for me?
questions.a: Studies of ribociclib with hormone therapy in defined advanced-breast-cancer groups showed a survival benefit. items.title: Who this treatment is for
items.text: HR-positive/HER2-negative locally advanced or metastatic disease with an AI or fulvestrant in the exact NCCP indication. NCCP page 1 and page 2 do not fully align on menopause and previous advanced-disease treatment; preserve consultant reconciliation.

items.title: Schedule and duration
items.text: The usual metastatic starting dose is ribociclib 600 mg once daily on Days 1–21 followed by Days 22–28 off. Continue the prescribed AI daily or fulvestrant on its own injection schedule; add ovarian suppression when indicated. Continue while beneficial and tolerated. chapters.title: Checks before and during treatment

items.title: Before the first dose
items.text: FBC, renal and liver profile, potassium, calcium, magnesium and phosphorus. ECG before initiation; QTcF must be below 450 ms. Correct electrolyte abnormalities and review QT/CYP3A interactions. Confirm endocrine partner, menopause/ovarian suppression, prior treatment and the NCCP indication/eligibility discrepancy.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: FBC, renal and liver profile every two weeks for cycles 1–2, then before cycles 3–6, then as clinically indicated. Electrolytes before each of the first six cycles, then as clinically indicated; correct abnormalities. Repeat ECG around Day 14 of cycle 1, then as clinically indicated. Increase liver monitoring for grade 2 or worse abnormalities. Review fever, jaundice, palpitations/fainting, pulmonary and severe skin symptoms; response imaging follows the advanced-disease plan.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: Supportive medicines and the endocrine partner have their own plan.

items.title: Nausea support
items.text: NCCP classifies ribociclib as oral moderate–high emetic risk. The team chooses preventive or rescue antiemetics using local policy, symptoms, QT risk and drug interactions; do not reuse another regimen’s prescription.

items.title: Electrolytes and heart rhythm
items.text: Correct abnormal potassium, calcium, magnesium and phosphate as directed. Attend the baseline and cycle 1 Day-14 ECG; fainting or palpitations need urgent advice.

items.title: Counts and liver tests
items.text: Keep the early two-weekly blood tests and subsequent monitoring. Report fever, shivers, jaundice or dark urine promptly.

items.title: Endocrine treatment
items.text: The AI or fulvestrant, and ovarian suppression when prescribed, continue on their own timetable. Discuss joint, menopausal, bone and injection-site symptoms.

items.title: Daily administration
items.text: Avoid grapefruit and check interactions. Do not replace a missed or vomited dose. A clinical hold requires explicit instructions about which medicine stops and who authorises restart.

sections.text: Confirm the exact medicine, strength, endocrine partner, baseline tests and first review appointments. Ask who arranges tests and who reviews the results.

sections.title: Taking treatment
sections.text: Take ribociclib once daily with or without food; swallow whole. Avoid grapefruit. If a dose is missed or vomited, do not take an extra dose; take the next scheduled dose. Confirm any clinical hold and restart with the team. The endocrine partner follows a separate prescription.

sections.title: Your endocrine partner has a separate timetable
sections.text: An aromatase inhibitor is normally taken daily through the targeted-medicine rest week. If fulvestrant is the chosen partner, the usual schedule is 500 mg by intramuscular injection on Days 1, 15 and 29, then once monthly; confirm the prescribed dose and appointment dates. Any ovarian-suppression injections have their own schedule.

sections.title: Supply and appointments
sections.text: Request the next supply before tablets run out. Blood tests and any ECG or injections need their own appointments. This oral treatment does not itself require a central line or infusion pump.

sections.title: If treatment is held
sections.text: Ask which medicine is held, whether the endocrine partner continues, what needs to recover, when the next review is due and who will authorise restart.

sections.title: Support between appointments
sections.text: Keep the oncology contact details and prescribed symptom medicines accessible. New severe symptoms need prompt assessment rather than waiting for the next blood test.

clinical.component_rationale: Ribociclib: Ribociclib blocks CDK4 and CDK6, proteins that help cells move through the cycle of division. Endocrine therapy reduces the hormone signal that can drive HR-positive breast cancer. AI or fulvestrant: An aromatase inhibitor (AI) lowers oestrogen production; fulvestrant blocks and reduces oestrogen receptors. These are alternative endocrine partners, selected by the team. Ovarian suppression is needed in pre/perimenopausal patients.

agents.name: Abemaciclib
agents.explanation: Abemaciclib inhibits CDK4 and CDK6 proteins. These proteins help cells move towards division. It is combined with endocrine treatment to reduce recurrence risk in eligible high-risk early breast cancer.
agents.watch: Start the prescribed diarrhoea rescue plan at the first loose stool and contact the team. Breathlessness, a swollen painful leg, fever or jaundice need prompt assessment.

agents.name: Your endocrine treatment
agents.explanation: The chosen endocrine medicine either reduces oestrogen production or blocks its action. An aromatase inhibitor may need ovarian suppression before menopause. The exact drug and duration are prescribed separately.
agents.watch: Tell the team about joint pain, hot flushes, vaginal symptoms and mood changes. The bone-health and clot-risk discussion depends on the drug chosen.

patient.phases_note: A general pathway, not an appointment calendar. Your team confirms the order, overlap and duration; no date entry is needed.
patient.timeline_note: Treatment bands show the source schedule. Symptom bands show possible patterns, not measured probabilities; serious effects can occur at any time.
patient.safety_note: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell require immediate contact. Serious symptoms override the timeline or diary.
patient.teachback: Which medicine is taken when, which test is due next, who reviews it, and which symptoms mean you should call today?
patient.consent_support: Discuss the treatment aim, alternatives, benefit and uncertainty, important medicine-specific risks, reproductive precautions, symptom support and planned duration. Confirm the endocrine partner and any ovarian-suppression plan. The timeline does not authorise a restart or certify clinical review.
patient.urgent_extra: Report new breathlessness, chest symptoms, severe diarrhoea, inability to drink, jaundice, a painful swollen leg or a severe rash promptly. You do not need to identify which medicine caused the symptom.

support.title: Diarrhoea rescue from the first loose stool
support.text: Have the prescribed antidiarrhoeal treatment available before starting. Begin the agreed plan at the first loose stool, increase fluids as advised and contact the team early; persistent symptoms or dehydration may require a treatment hold.

support.title: Nausea support
support.text: NCCP classifies abemaciclib as oral moderate–high emetic risk. Agree preventive or rescue antiemetics using individual risk and local oral-SACT policy.

support.title: Blood, liver and symptom checks
support.text: Attend early two-weekly then monthly checks even when tablets are taken at home. Seek prompt advice for infection, jaundice, new breathing symptoms or possible blood clots.

support.title: Endocrine and bone support
support.text: Discuss symptoms and bone protection for the actual endocrine partner. Ovarian suppression is required with an AI before menopause. Endocrine treatment normally continues after the two-year abemaciclib course.

support.title: Medicines and supply
support.text: Take tablets whole at the prescribed regular times. There is no routine week off. Check grapefruit/CYP3A interactions and do not double a missed or vomited dose.

questions.q: How long does treatment last?
questions.a: The usual abemaciclib starting dose is 150 mg twice daily; a lower dose or altered schedule may be prescribed. Abemaciclib is taken twice daily continuously for up to two years with endocrine therapy, unless recurrence or unacceptable toxicity requires an earlier change. A four-week dispensing block is not a rest cycle. Endocrine treatment normally continues beyond abemaciclib. At completion of the planned two-year abemaciclib course, continue the separately agreed endocrine and follow-up plan.

questions.q: Which checks happen before and during treatment?
questions.a: FBC, renal, liver and bone profile; ECG as clinically indicated. Confirm node-positive high-risk eligibility, definitive surgery and timing: within 16 months of resection and up to 12 weeks of endocrine treatment after the last non-endocrine treatment before starting. Assess VTE history, bowel function, all medicines, endocrine partner, ovarian suppression if using an AI before menopause, and bone/reproductive health. FBC, renal, liver and bone profile every two weeks for the first two months, monthly for the next two months, then as clinically indicated. More frequent liver monitoring for grade 2 or worse liver abnormalities. ECG is driven by clinical need; no routine ribociclib Day-14 ECG schedule. Early and ongoing diarrhoea review, hydration/intake, infection, clots, breathlessness and adherence; prompt action between appointments. Creatinine can rise through inhibited tubular secretion without a true fall in filtration; assess the clinical context and alternative renal measures if needed.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates?
questions.a: No. This map shows general timing without personal information. Your hospital arranges actual appointments; ask who books each test and who reviews its result.

questions.q: What if a dose is missed or treatment is held?
questions.a: Take abemaciclib twice daily at regular times with or without food. Swallow whole; do not split, chew or crush. Avoid grapefruit. Do not replace a missed or vomited dose. A clinical hold and restart require the treating team’s instructions. A hold may affect one medicine rather than the whole combination; confirm each component.

questions.q: What does the evidence mean for me?
questions.a: Adding a planned course of abemaciclib to endocrine therapy reduced the chance of invasive cancer returning in eligible high-risk, node-positive early breast cancer. Longer follow-up also showed an overall-survival benefit. These group results do not predict your own outcome.

questions.q: What happens after treatment changes or ends?
questions.a: At completion of the planned two-year abemaciclib course, continue the separately agreed endocrine and follow-up plan. Keep the separately agreed disease follow-up, endocrine and bone-health plan.

evidence.trial: monarchE: primary OS and seven-year outcomes
evidence.population: 5,637 patients with HR-positive/HER2-negative, node-positive high-risk early breast cancer; intention-to-treat trial population. NCCP00619 uses its specified clinicopathological high-risk criteria.
evidence.comparison: Two years of abemaciclib plus endocrine therapy versus endocrine therapy alone; endocrine therapy planned for at least five years.
evidence.applicability: Adjuvant recurrence prevention after definitive surgery. Do not extend to node-negative disease or replace NCCP timing and high-risk criteria with the broader trial label.
evidence.qualitative_result: The primary OS analysis met the prespecified significance boundary; invasive and distant recurrence benefits persisted after the two-year abemaciclib course.

endpoints.metric: Estimated overall survival at seven years
endpoints.result_text: 86.8% versus 85.0%; absolute difference 1.8 percentage points. HR 0.842 (95% CI 0.722–0.981), P=.027.
endpoints.interpretation: The primary OS analysis met its prespecified significance boundary.
endpoints.analysis_status: Primary OS analysis; 661 deaths, median follow-up 76.2 months; published online October 2025

endpoints.interpretation: The invasive recurrence/death composite remained improved after treatment ended.
endpoints.analysis_status: Updated seven-year efficacy analysis accompanying primary OS

support.title: Nausea support

support.title: Heart rhythm and electrolytes
support.text: Attend the baseline and cycle 1 Day-14 ECG and scheduled electrolyte checks. Fainting, palpitations or severe dizziness need urgent assessment.

support.title: Blood and liver monitoring
support.text: Keep two-weekly blood tests during cycles 1–2 and pre-cycle tests during cycles 3–6. Report fever, jaundice, dark urine or new breathing/skin symptoms promptly.

support.title: AI and ovarian-suppression support
support.text: The aromatase inhibitor continues during the ribociclib rest week and generally after ribociclib completion. Discuss menopause, joints, sexual health, bone risk and any injection-site symptoms from ovarian suppression.

support.title: Completion and follow-up
support.text: Ribociclib has a planned maximum three-year course. Confirm the endocrine duration and early-breast surveillance plan separately; new symptoms should be assessed without waiting for a routine appointment.

questions.q: How long does treatment last?
questions.a: The usual adjuvant starting dose is ribociclib 400 mg once daily on Days 1–21, followed by Days 22–28 off, for up to three years. The aromatase inhibitor continues every day on its own plan; ovarian suppression is added when indicated. At completion of the planned three-year ribociclib course, continue the separately agreed endocrine and follow-up plan.

questions.q: Which checks happen before and during treatment?
questions.a: FBC, renal and liver profile; potassium, calcium, magnesium and phosphorus. ECG before initiation; QTcF must be below 450 ms. Correct electrolytes and review QT/CYP3A interactions. Confirm stage, recurrence-risk criteria, prior treatment, AI and ovarian-suppression plan; reconcile the NCCP node-negative eligibility/exclusion conflict before selection. FBC, renal and liver profile every two weeks for cycles 1–2, then before cycles 3–6, then as clinically indicated. Electrolytes before each of the first six cycles, then as clinically indicated. Repeat ECG around cycle 1 Day 14, then as clinically indicated. Increase liver monitoring for grade 2 or worse abnormalities; review fever, jaundice, palpitations/fainting, breathlessness and severe skin symptoms. Keep early-breast surveillance and bone/endocrine follow-up distinct from treatment-toxicity checks and from metastatic response imaging.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates?
questions.a: No. This map shows general timing without personal information. Your hospital arranges actual appointments; ask who books each test and who reviews its result.

questions.q: What if a dose is missed or treatment is held?
questions.a: Take ribociclib once daily with or without food; swallow whole. Avoid grapefruit. If a dose is missed or vomited, do not take an extra dose; take the next scheduled dose. Confirm any clinical hold and restart with the team. The endocrine partner follows a separate prescription. A hold may affect one medicine rather than the whole combination; confirm each component.

questions.q: What does the evidence mean for me?
questions.a: Ribociclib added to an aromatase inhibitor reduced the chance of invasive cancer returning in the study. Recent longer follow-up also reported a favorable survival finding, but that analysis was descriptive and needs that qualification. Your treatment team can explain how the study matches your recurrence risk.

questions.q: What happens after treatment changes or ends?
questions.a: At completion of the planned three-year ribociclib course, continue the separately agreed endocrine and follow-up plan. Keep the separately agreed disease follow-up, endocrine and bone-health plan.

evidence.applicability: Adjuvant population; not MONALEESA metastatic evidence. NCCP00892v2 includes selected node-negative eligibility but also a conflicting node-negative exclusion, which still requires clinical reconciliation.
evidence.qualitative_result: The primary trial established an iDFS benefit. The six-year descriptive analysis continued to favor ribociclib for recurrence outcomes and reported a favorable OS estimate with a nominal P value.

support_plans.label: Adjuvant ribociclib + endocrine therapy · supportive-care plan
additional_support: NCCP classifies ribociclib as oral moderate–high emetic risk. Agree preventive or rescue treatment under local policy after QT and CYP3A interaction review; no default QT-prolonging antiemetic is selected by this information card.
Attend the baseline and cycle 1 Day-14 ECG and scheduled electrolyte checks. Fainting, palpitations or severe dizziness need urgent assessment.
Keep two-weekly blood tests during cycles 1–2 and pre-cycle tests during cycles 3–6. Report fever, jaundice, dark urine or new breathing/skin symptoms promptly.

The aromatase inhibitor continues during the ribociclib rest week and generally after ribociclib completion. Discuss menopause, joints, sexual health, bone risk and any injection-site symptoms from ovarian suppression.

Ribociclib has a planned maximum three-year course. Confirm the endocrine duration and early-breast surveillance plan separately; new symptoms should be assessed without waiting for a routine appointment.

support.title: Support for this medicine
support.text: Trastuzumab alone has minimal emetogenic risk. Routine chemotherapy antiemetics, steroids and growth factors are not added automatically. Previous reactions require a separate plan.

support.title: Blood and heart appointments
support.text: FBC, renal and liver profile every 6 weeks (around C3, C5, C7 if on time). Echo / MUGA every 12 weeks; around C5 for uninterrupted 21-day cycles.

support.title: Local treatment and endocrine therapy
support.text: Surgery and radiotherapy are coordinated by the MDT. When endocrine therapy is indicated, it has its own schedule and bone-health plan.

support.title: Pregnancy / contraception
support.text: Discuss pregnancy, fertility and contraception before treatment. Report pregnancy promptly; do not breastfeed during treatment or for 7 months afterwards. The team confirms the medicine-specific contraception duration.

questions.q: How long will I receive treatment?
questions.a: Trastuzumab 600 mg under the skin every 21 days, without a loading dose, while beneficial and tolerated. Any taxane or endocrine partner follows a separate prescription and monitoring plan.

questions.q: When is my next echo?
questions.a: Echo / MUGA every 12 weeks; around C5 for uninterrupted 21-day cycles. Existing HER2 exposure and delays affect cycle numbering; the team should give the actual due window.

questions.q: How does radiotherapy fit?
questions.a: Radiotherapy is used for a defined site or symptom when indicated. The oncology and radiation teams agree whether this medicine continues or pauses; do not infer a concurrent schedule from this card.

questions.q: Does a tumour marker replace a scan?
questions.a: No. In metastatic disease it may add information to symptoms and imaging. It should not alone determine treatment changes. In symptom-free early disease it is not routine recurrence screening.

evidence.title: Trastuzumab formulation evidence
evidence.intro: This explains the study setting and its meaning. Ask the team how the evidence applies to you.
evidence.population: HannaH compared under-the-skin and intravenous trastuzumab with chemotherapy in early breast cancer.
evidence.interpretation: Longer follow-up found similar outcomes with the two formulations. This study helps explain the choice of route; it does not predict your own outcome. Its early-cancer outcomes cannot be used as a metastatic survival estimate.

evidence.population: 596 randomised patients with HER2-positive early, locally advanced or inflammatory breast cancer; neoadjuvant chemotherapy plus SC or IV trastuzumab followed by postoperative trastuzumab to complete one year.
evidence.comparison: SC trastuzumab 600 mg versus weight-based IV trastuzumab; both groups received chemotherapy.
evidence.applicability: Indirect formulation evidence only. HannaH is not a metastatic trial and supplies no metastatic survival estimate.
evidence.qualitative_result: Long-term event-free and overall survival were similar between formulations; these results do not quantify benefit over omitting trastuzumab.

endpoints.interpretation: Early-disease formulation comparison; no metastatic efficacy attribution.
endpoints.analysis_status: Final six-year analysis, secondary endpoint; initial coprimary endpoints were drug exposure and pathological complete response.

questions.q: How long will I receive treatment?
questions.a: Trastuzumab 600 mg under the skin every 21 days, without a loading dose, to complete one year total. Previous IV or combination-treatment trastuzumab counts towards that year; a route switch does not start a new year.

questions.q: When is my next echo?
questions.a: Echo / MUGA every 12 weeks; around C5 for uninterrupted 21-day cycles. Existing HER2 exposure and delays affect cycle numbering; the team should give the actual due window.

questions.q: How does radiotherapy fit?

questions.q: Does a tumour marker replace a scan?

patient.context_label: Unresectable or metastatic HER2-positive or HER2-low breast cancer, within the NCCP prior-treatment criteria
patient.schedule_summary: One infusion on Day 1 of a 21-day cycle. The next infusion is normally three weeks later. A delayed appointment is rescheduled by the team; patients do not calculate catch-up doses.
patient.purpose: Aim to control cancer growth, reduce cancer-related symptoms and prolong disease control. Individual benefit and duration vary; trial averages cannot predict one person's outcome.
patient.indication_text: NCCP00776a: unresectable/metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer after at least one anti-HER2 regimen. NCCP00776b: unresectable/metastatic HER2-low breast cancer after chemotherapy for metastatic disease, or recurrence during or within six months after adjuvant chemotherapy.
patient.administration_text: The first infusion takes 90 minutes. Later infusions may take 30 minutes if the previous infusion was tolerated. Allow extra time for assessment, anti-sickness medicines and any observation. A cannula or an existing central line can be used according to the clinical plan; there is no home pump.
patient.monitoring_summary: Before the first dose: full blood count, kidney and liver tests, an echocardiogram or MUGA scan to measure heart pumping function, and a pregnancy test where relevant. The team checks the HER2 result, previous treatment, lung history and current breathing symptoms, and agrees how disease response will be assessed. Blood count, kidney and liver tests before each 21-day cycle. Review breathing, fatigue, nausea, intake and other symptoms at each visit. Repeat cardiac imaging every 12 weeks; assess new breathing symptoms immediately rather than waiting for the next planned scan.

agents.name: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (Enhertu)
agents.mechanism: Uses HER2 as a docking target to deliver a topoisomerase-I inhibitor payload
visual: Cancer cell takes the linked drug inside
Released payload damages DNA during cell division
agents.explanation: Enhertu links an antibody that recognises HER2 with deruxtecan, a cell-killing medicine. After uptake into the cell, the payload inhibits topoisomerase I and interferes with DNA replication. The released payload can also affect nearby tumour cells. This targeting does not spare every healthy cell, which is why blood counts, nausea, lungs and heart function still need attention.
agents.watch: New cough, breathlessness or fever needs urgent contact even between cycles. Keep the 12-weekly heart-scan plan and use the anti-sickness medicines as prescribed.
risks: Nausea and vomiting, including delayed symptoms
Fatigue, reduced appetite and hair loss
Low blood counts: infection, anaemia or bleeding
Interstitial lung disease / pneumonitis, sometimes fatal
Reduced heart pumping function or heart failure
Harm to an unborn baby and possible fertility effects

sections.title: Before each visit
sections.text: Have the requested blood tests and report any new breathing symptoms before attending for treatment. Bring your medication list and the Enhertu alert card. Ask when your next heart scan is due.

sections.title: On infusion day
sections.text: Take the prescribed anti-sickness medicines as instructed. The infusion is longer the first time. Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, chills, rash, dizziness, wheeze or breathing difficulty during treatment.

sections.title: Between infusions
sections.text: Nausea can continue after treatment day. Follow the scheduled and rescue anti-sickness plan, drink regularly and contact the team early if vomiting prevents fluid intake. Keep activity manageable and ask for help with fatigue.

sections.title: Scans answer different questions
sections.text: Echo/MUGA monitors heart pumping function. Cancer-response scans follow the oncology plan. A CT requested urgently for new cough or breathlessness investigates a possible treatment complication; it must not wait for a routine response scan.

sections.title: If you already have a port
sections.text: A trained nurse accesses and removes the port needle for the infusion visit, then flushes the line according to local policy. Report redness, pain, swelling or fever. A new port is an individual decision, not compulsory for everyone receiving Enhertu.

evidence.title: Evidence for HER2-positive and HER2-low advanced breast cancer
evidence.population: Separate studies enrolled people with previously treated HER2-positive or HER2-low advanced breast cancer.
evidence.primary_endpoint: Primary endpoint: blinded-central-review PFS, previously reported. This update reports investigator-assessed PFS and overall survival.
evidence.interpretation: Trastuzumab deruxtecan delayed cancer growth and improved survival compared with the treatments studied. The two studies involved different cancer groups and should not be combined into a personal prediction. Benefits must be considered alongside lung inflammation and other side effects.
evidence.limitations: Randomised open-label trial in a selected prior-treatment population. This PFS estimate is investigator assessed and must not be mislabeled as the original primary-endpoint analysis. Population medians are not individual forecasts. All-grade ILD/pneumonitis was 16.7% with T-DXd in this longer follow-up.
evidence.intro: This explains the study setting and its meaning. Ask the team how the evidence applies to you.
evidence.comparison_label: The comparator depended on the study and cancer type.

patient.teachback: Which medicine is taken or given when, what checks are expected next, and which symptoms mean you should call today?
patient.consent_support: Enhertu is different from trastuzumab and trastuzumab emtansine (Kadcyla); they are not interchangeable. Carry the supplied Enhertu lung-safety alert card. The team may pause treatment while investigating suspected lung inflammation; symptomatic drug-related ILD requires permanent discontinuation under the protocol. Where relevant, use effective contraception during treatment and for at least seven months after the last dose for women, or four months for men with a partner who could become pregnant. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for seven months after the last dose. Discuss fertility before starting.

support.title: Prevent nausea before it starts
support.text: This regimen has high emetic risk. An antiemetic combination is prescribed before every infusion, with an agreed plan for delayed symptoms and breakthrough nausea. The dedicated NCCP trastuzumab-deruxtecan pathway should be checked by the prescriber and pharmacist.

support.title: Lung-safety plan
support.text: Carry the patient alert card and report new cough, fever or breathlessness promptly. Steroids used for suspected lung inflammation are prescribed and monitored by the clinical team; do not start them yourself from this information.

support.title: Blood-count support
support.text: Low blood counts can cause infection, anaemia or bleeding. The need for G-CSF or transfusion support depends on results, symptoms and previous complications; it is not automatic for every cycle.

support.title: Eating and energy
support.text: Small frequent meals and early treatment of nausea can help maintain intake. Tell the team about weight loss, constipation or diarrhoea so that support can be tailored.

timeline.label: Nausea may be delayed

timeline.label: Energy and blood counts
