chapters.title: The exact treatment being discussed
chapters.intro: Aim to control cancer growth, reduce cancer-related symptoms and prolong disease control. Individual benefit and duration vary; trial averages cannot predict one person's outcome.

items.title: Who this covers
items.text: NCCP00776a: unresectable/metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer after at least one anti-HER2 regimen. NCCP00776b: unresectable/metastatic HER2-low breast cancer after chemotherapy for metastatic disease, or recurrence during or within six months after adjuvant chemotherapy.

items.title: Dose and administration
items.text: Usual starting dose 5.4 mg/kg intravenously on Day 1 every 21 days; prescribed reductions are 4.4 then 3.2 mg/kg. The first infusion takes 90 minutes. Later infusions may take 30 minutes if the previous infusion was tolerated. Allow extra time for assessment, anti-sickness medicines and any observation. A cannula or an existing central line can be used according to the clinical plan; there is no home pump.

items.title: Duration and decisions
items.text: Treatment continues while it controls the cancer and side effects remain acceptable. This advanced-disease regimen has no automatic one-year completion date. A good scan does not by itself instruct a treatment break.

items.title: Individual safety and source differences
items.text: Enhertu is different from trastuzumab and trastuzumab emtansine (Kadcyla); they are not interchangeable. Carry the supplied Enhertu lung-safety alert card. The team may pause treatment while investigating suspected lung inflammation; symptomatic drug-related ILD requires permanent discontinuation under the protocol.

chapters.title: Checks throughout treatment
chapters.intro: Blood tests assess treatment safety. Scans assess disease or investigate symptoms. Echo and ECG answer different questions.

items.title: Before treatment
items.text: Before the first dose: full blood count, kidney and liver tests, an echocardiogram or MUGA scan to measure heart pumping function, and a pregnancy test where relevant. The team checks the HER2 result, previous treatment, lung history and current breathing symptoms, and agrees how disease response will be assessed.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: Blood count, kidney and liver tests before each 21-day cycle. Review breathing, fatigue, nausea, intake and other symptoms at each visit. Repeat cardiac imaging every 12 weeks; assess new breathing symptoms immediately rather than waiting for the next planned scan.

items.title: Heart checks
items.text: NCCP specifies echo/MUGA before treatment and every 12 weeks. With uninterrupted three-week cycles, week 12 is approximately before cycle 5 and week 24 before cycle 9. Delays do not reset the elapsed-time monitoring clock. Signs of cardiac impairment can require 4–8-weekly checks; an abnormal result meeting the treatment-hold criteria requires repeat assessment within three weeks.

items.title: Bone health
items.text: Enhertu alone does not require a routine bone-density scan schedule. DEXA, bone medicines or bone scans are added for another treatment, fracture risk, symptoms or disease assessment when indicated.

chapters.title: Your wider treatment plan
chapters.intro: Additional treatments depend on the confirmed setting and indication.

items.title: Advanced-disease scans
items.text: Response assessment in advanced breast cancer is generally every two to four months, adapted to disease dynamics, sites, symptoms and treatment. Less frequent monitoring may suit indolent disease. New symptoms or suspected progression need earlier assessment. The team chooses the imaging method; this is not an automatic three-month CT chest/abdomen/pelvis order.

items.title: Tumour markers
items.text: If informative, particularly when elevated at baseline or disease is not readily measurable, tumour markers may supplement clinical assessment and imaging. A marker rise alone should not trigger a treatment change. There is no universal fixed marker timetable.

items.title: Pregnancy, fertility and contraception
items.text: Where relevant, use effective contraception during treatment and for at least seven months after the last dose for women, or four months for men with a partner who could become pregnant. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for seven months after the last dose. Discuss fertility before starting.

chapters.title: Evidence depends on the population
chapters.intro: Different studies answer different questions; do not compare their results as if populations and follow-up were identical.

items.title: DESTINY-Breast04: previously treated HER2-low advanced breast cancer
items.text: 557 patients with HER2-low metastatic breast cancer after one or two previous chemotherapy lines; 494 had hormone-receptor-positive disease. T-DXd versus physician's-choice chemotherapy. Blinded-central-review PFS in the hormone-receptor-positive cohort; PFS and OS in all patients were key secondary endpoints. In the HR-positive cohort, median PFS was 10.1 versus 5.4 months (HR 0.51). In all patients, median PFS was 9.9 versus 5.1 months (HR 0.50) and median OS 23.4 versus 16.8 months (HR 0.64). These are the original 2022 analysis, also reproduced in EMA SmPC §5.1. The HR-negative subgroup was much smaller. The trial does not establish benefit for HER2 IHC0 tumours or every earlier treatment setting. Drug-related ILD/pneumonitis occurred, including fatal cases; benefit must be discussed alongside pulmonary risk.

clinical.component_rationale: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (Enhertu): Enhertu links an antibody that recognises HER2 with deruxtecan, a cell-killing medicine. After uptake into the cell, the payload inhibits topoisomerase I and interferes with DNA replication. The released payload can also affect nearby tumour cells. This targeting does not spare every healthy cell, which is why blood counts, nausea, lungs and heart function still need attention.

NCCP00776v3b remains the eligibility anchor despite broader EMA indications. Do not silently add first-line pertuzumab combinations, HER2-ultralow, other tissue sites or earlier-line HER2-low use.
Every12-week echo is an elapsed-time interval; cycle5/9 mapping assumes uninterrupted21-day dosing. New dysfunction changes the interval and treatment decision.
Grade1 ILD restart needs complete Grade0 resolution; ≤28days permits the same dose and >28days a reduction. Symptomatic Grade≥2 ILD requires permanent discontinuation and prompt corticosteroids.

NCCP expects no dose adjustment in severe renal impairment/dialysis; EMA says requirements cannot be determined. Moderate hepatic impairment also has a source-language difference. The engine flags specialist/pharmacy reconciliation rather than inventing a numeric dose.
Neither current NCCP nor the retrieved EMA SmPC supplies a platelet-specific dose ladder. FBC review remains mandatory; US-label thrombocytopenia instructions are not silently substituted.
NCCP eligibility says age>18 while the indication and EMA say adults. The age18 boundary is flagged for clinical/pharmacy interpretation.
Routine prophylactic steroids for antiemesis and high-dose treatment for ILD serve different purposes; patient information must not imply self-starting ILD steroids.

rationale.summary: Trastuzumab deruxtecan delivers a topoisomerase-I-inhibiting payload through HER2 binding to control selected advanced breast cancer. HER2-positive and HER2-low indications have separate prior-treatment criteria.
rationale.setting: Unresectable or metastatic HER2-positive after one or more anti-HER2 regimens, or HER2-low after metastatic chemotherapy or relapse during/within six months after adjuvant chemotherapy, under NCCP00776v3b.
rationale.line: NCCP indication-specific prior treatment; not an automatic first-line or early-stage pathway.
factors: Confirm the exact HER2 category and prior treatment.
Review lung history, new respiratory symptoms, baseline cardiac function, blood counts and organ function.
Plan preventive antiemetics, lung-safety alert-card education and a clear urgent contact route.
Reassess benefit and safety every cycle; no fixed one-year course in this advanced-disease regimen.
alternatives: Other HER2-directed or cytotoxic options depend on phenotype, prior exposure, CNS disease, toxicity and preferences. Comparisons between different trials do not establish a ranking.
limitations: DESTINY-Breast03 HER2-positive results and DESTINY-Breast04 HER2-low results must remain separate.
Updated PFS reported below is investigator assessed, distinct from the earlier primary BICR analysis.
Broader current EMA indications do not automatically expand the NCCP00776v3b catalogue entry.
NCCP eligibility wording referring to HER2 overexpression must be read alongside its explicit HER2-low indication; do not erase the HER2-low branch.
Independent clinical/pharmacy/PPI approval is pending.

Grade1 ILD restart needs complete Grade0 resolution; ≤28days permits the same dose and >28days a reduction. Symptomatic Grade≥2 ILD requires permanent discontinuation and prompt corticosteroids.

NCCP expects no dose adjustment in severe renal impairment/dialysis; EMA says requirements cannot be determined. Moderate hepatic impairment also has a source-language difference. The engine flags specialist/pharmacy reconciliation rather than inventing a numeric dose.
Neither current NCCP nor the retrieved EMA SmPC supplies a platelet-specific dose ladder. FBC review remains mandatory; US-label thrombocytopenia instructions are not silently substituted.
NCCP eligibility says age>18 while the indication and EMA say adults. The age18 boundary is flagged for clinical/pharmacy interpretation.
Routine prophylactic steroids for antiemesis and high-dose treatment for ILD serve different purposes; patient information must not imply self-starting ILD steroids.

Enhertu is different from trastuzumab and trastuzumab emtansine (Kadcyla); they are not interchangeable. Carry the supplied Enhertu lung-safety alert card. The team may pause treatment while investigating suspected lung inflammation; symptomatic drug-related ILD requires permanent discontinuation under the protocol.

Where relevant, use effective contraception during treatment and for at least seven months after the last dose for women, or four months for men with a partner who could become pregnant. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for seven months after the last dose. Discuss fertility before starting.

NCCP specifies echo/MUGA before treatment and every 12 weeks. With uninterrupted three-week cycles, week 12 is approximately before cycle 5 and week 24 before cycle 9. Delays do not reset the elapsed-time monitoring clock. Signs of cardiac impairment can require 4–8-weekly checks; an abnormal result meeting the treatment-hold criteria requires repeat assessment within three weeks.
Enhertu alone does not require a routine bone-density scan schedule. DEXA, bone medicines or bone scans are added for another treatment, fracture risk, symptoms or disease assessment when indicated.

Response assessment in advanced breast cancer is generally every two to four months, adapted to disease dynamics, sites, symptoms and treatment. Less frequent monitoring may suit indolent disease. New symptoms or suspected progression need earlier assessment. The team chooses the imaging method; this is not an automatic three-month CT chest/abdomen/pelvis order.

If informative, particularly when elevated at baseline or disease is not readily measurable, tumour markers may supplement clinical assessment and imaging. A marker rise alone should not trigger a treatment change. There is no universal fixed marker timetable.

agents.name: Sacituzumab govitecan (Trodelvy)
agents.mechanism: Carries the topoisomerase-I inhibitor SN-38 using an antibody that recognises Trop-2
agents.explanation: The antibody component recognises Trop-2 on cancer cells. Its linked SN-38 payload interferes with topoisomerase I, an enzyme involved in managing DNA during copying, which can damage dividing cells. Healthy tissues can also be affected, particularly blood-forming cells and the gut; being antibody-directed does not mean it is free of chemotherapy-type effects.
agents.watch: The most important early problems to act on are fever or infection with low neutrophils, diarrhoea and dehydration, persistent nausea/vomiting, and infusion reactions. Report symptoms early rather than waiting for a planned scan or clinic.
risks: Low neutrophils and serious infection, including febrile neutropenia
Diarrhoea, dehydration and electrolyte loss; sometimes kidney injury
Infusion reactions, including rare life-threatening reactions
Potential harm to an unborn baby and effects on fertility

sections.title: Plan two visits per cycle
sections.text: Day 1 and Day 8 are treatment days. Allow time for blood review, premedicines, the infusion and at least 30 minutes of observation afterwards. The first infusion is longer than later ones.

sections.title: Cannula or existing venous access
sections.text: The team chooses suitable intravenous access. A port is not automatically required and this regimen has no take-home pump. If you already have a port, staff access and flush it according to local policy; report pain, redness or swelling.

sections.title: Before leaving the unit
sections.text: Confirm the Day 8 appointment, blood-test arrangements, nausea medicines, written diarrhoea instructions and the number to call if unwell. If G-CSF is prescribed, ask exactly which days to take it around both treatment visits.

sections.title: If treatment is delayed
sections.text: A low count or significant side effect can mean a delay or dose change. The team will give the revised plan; do not calculate a replacement infusion from this diagram.

sections.title: If radiotherapy is also planned
sections.text: Radiotherapy is not an automatic phase of this advanced-disease regimen. If needed for local symptoms or another reason, the oncology and radiotherapy teams agree its timing and any treatment interruption.

evidence.title: ASCENT evidence in previously treated triple-negative breast cancer
evidence.population: ASCENT studied people with metastatic triple-negative breast cancer after previous treatment.
evidence.primary_endpoint: Progression-free survival by blinded independent central review in the population without baseline brain metastases.
evidence.interpretation: Sacituzumab delayed cancer growth and improved survival in the trial. The main early analysis and the later full-study analysis used different patient groups, so their results are described separately in the clinical evidence. Your benefit and side effects may differ from the study averages.
evidence.limitations: The primary analysis excluded baseline brain metastases; the overall-population estimates differ. Open-label design, selected trial fitness and previous-treatment requirements limit extrapolation. Group medians do not predict an individual patient's benefit. This trial does not establish eligibility for every broader current EU indication.
evidence.intro: This explains the study setting and its meaning. Ask the team how the evidence applies to you.
evidence.comparison_label: One of several standard single chemotherapy medicines.

patient.teachback: Which medicine is taken or given when, what checks are expected next, and which symptoms mean you should call today?

NCCP00794a is later-line unresectable/metastatic TNBC. Do not import current EU HR-positive, first-line or pembrolizumab-combination indications without the appropriate separate NCCP/reimbursement mapping.
Day 1 ANC threshold is ≥1.5 ×10⁹/L; Day 8 is ≥1.0 ×10⁹/L. An isolated ANC <1.0 can trigger a hold without a day; 1.0–<1.5 requires day context rather than a false clearance.

NCCP high-emetic-risk prophylaxis must cover BOTH Day 1 and Day 8. The suggested dexamethasone 12 mg infusion premedicine also provides antiemetic cover; reconcile with the selected high-risk script to prevent duplication.

NCCP suggested infusion premedicines: paracetamol 1 g PO 60 minutes beforehand; chlorphenamine 10 mg IV, famotidine 20 mg IV and dexamethasone 12 mg PO 30 minutes beforehand. Product availability, contraindications and local prescriptions must be checked.

Primary G-CSF should be considered from cycle 1 for increased-risk patients in the current EU SmPC. Product and timing must account for Day 1 and Day 8; do not automatically generate a single generic pegfilgrastim date.

NCCP advises considering a lower initial dose for known UGT1A1*28 homozygosity and possible escalation based on cycle-1 tolerance, but gives no fixed starting reduction. The EU SmPC recommends close monitoring and does not require routine genotype testing when status is unknown. Do not re-escalate a dose previously reduced because of adverse reactions.

NCCP Table 1 repeats 25% dose reduction at the second severe non-neutropenic event, whereas the current EU SmPC gives a 10→7.5→5 mg/kg ladder. The second-event output requires Consultant/pharmacy reconciliation and suppresses automatic numeric dosing.

NCCP Table 2 predicts no renal/hepatic adjustment across broad impairment bands. EU SmPC advises avoiding use when bilirubin >1.5×ULN or AST/ALT >3×ULN without liver metastases or >5×ULN with metastases, and notes absent severe/end-stage renal data. These differences are explicit in the assessment output.

NCCP contains >48-hour and >3-week toxicity-duration rules that differ from the current EU algorithm. Persisting severe toxicity must not be treated by merely calculating a reduced dose; recovery and source reconciliation are required.

NCCP's high-dose loperamide schedule is 4 mg initially then 2 mg every two hours, continued 12 hours after the last liquid stool and never beyond 48 consecutive hours at these doses because of ileus risk. The patient-facing page should direct to an individually prescribed local oncology plan rather than print an unsupervised automatic prescription. Assess infectious causes, fever, blood, severe pain and dehydration promptly.
Scan timing is Consultant-plan-specific; no universal three-month CT or tumour-marker schedule is specified in NCCP00794. Routine ECG/echo/DXA should not be added merely to fill a timeline.

rationale.summary: Sacituzumab govitecan targets Trop-2 to deliver the topoisomerase-I inhibitor SN-38, aiming to control previously treated metastatic triple-negative breast cancer.
rationale.setting: Unresectable or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer after at least two systemic therapies, including at least one for advanced disease, under NCCP00794v3.
rationale.line: Later-line TNBC within the NCCP prior-treatment criteria.
factors: Confirm triple-negative status and prior lines, including advanced-disease exposure.
Review Day 1 and Day 8 neutrophil thresholds separately.
Plan antiemetics, infusion premedication and a rapid diarrhoea/dehydration response.

alternatives: Other single-agent chemotherapy, biomarker-directed approaches or symptom-directed care depend on prior exposure and clinical context; ASCENT does not compare all current options.
limitations: The original ASCENT primary analysis excluded brain metastases; final overall-population results include the full randomised population. Do not mix their endpoint numbers.
Trop-2 testing was not an NCCP eligibility requirement and exploratory expression analyses do not create one.
Other EMA sacituzumab indications are not automatically part of NCCP00794v3.

NCCP severe non-neutropenic toxicity table repeats a 25% reduction on second occurrence; preserve the existing source discrepancy and require individual pharmacy confirmation rather than silently converting to the EMA dose-level table.
Independent clinical/pharmacy/PPI approval is pending.

drug_mechanisms.sacituzumab_govitecan: The antibody component recognises Trop-2 on cancer cells. Its linked SN-38 payload interferes with topoisomerase I, an enzyme involved in managing DNA during copying, which can damage dividing cells. Healthy tissues can also be affected, particularly blood-forming cells and the gut; being antibody-directed does not mean it is free of chemotherapy-type effects.

evidence.population: 529 patients with relapsed/refractory metastatic TNBC, 267 assigned sacituzumab and 262 physician-choice chemotherapy; prior chemotherapy including a taxane.
evidence.comparison: Sacituzumab govitecan versus eribulin, vinorelbine, capecitabine or gemcitabine.
evidence.applicability: Final full randomised population, distinct from the original 468-patient primary population without brain metastases.
evidence.qualitative_result: Sacituzumab improved disease control and survival compared with the trial chemotherapy options.

clinical_notes: NCCP00794a is later-line unresectable/metastatic TNBC. Do not import current EU HR-positive, first-line or pembrolizumab-combination indications without the appropriate separate NCCP/reimbursement mapping.
Day 1 ANC threshold is ≥1.5 ×10⁹/L; Day 8 is ≥1.0 ×10⁹/L. An isolated ANC <1.0 can trigger a hold without a day; 1.0–<1.5 requires day context rather than a false clearance.

NCCP high-emetic-risk prophylaxis must cover BOTH Day 1 and Day 8. The suggested dexamethasone 12 mg infusion premedicine also provides antiemetic cover; reconcile with the selected high-risk script to prevent duplication.

NCCP suggested infusion premedicines: paracetamol 1 g PO 60 minutes beforehand; chlorphenamine 10 mg IV, famotidine 20 mg IV and dexamethasone 12 mg PO 30 minutes beforehand. Product availability, contraindications and local prescriptions must be checked.

Primary G-CSF should be considered from cycle 1 for increased-risk patients in the current EU SmPC. Product and timing must account for Day 1 and Day 8; do not automatically generate a single generic pegfilgrastim date.

NCCP advises considering a lower initial dose for known UGT1A1*28 homozygosity and possible escalation based on cycle-1 tolerance, but gives no fixed starting reduction. The EU SmPC recommends close monitoring and does not require routine genotype testing when status is unknown. Do not re-escalate a dose previously reduced because of adverse reactions.

NCCP Table 1 repeats 25% dose reduction at the second severe non-neutropenic event, whereas the current EU SmPC gives a 10→7.5→5 mg/kg ladder. The second-event output requires Consultant/pharmacy reconciliation and suppresses automatic numeric dosing.

NCCP Table 2 predicts no renal/hepatic adjustment across broad impairment bands. EU SmPC advises avoiding use when bilirubin >1.5×ULN or AST/ALT >3×ULN without liver metastases or >5×ULN with metastases, and notes absent severe/end-stage renal data. These differences are explicit in the assessment output.

NCCP contains >48-hour and >3-week toxicity-duration rules that differ from the current EU algorithm. Persisting severe toxicity must not be treated by merely calculating a reduced dose; recovery and source reconciliation are required.

NCCP's high-dose loperamide schedule is 4 mg initially then 2 mg every two hours, continued 12 hours after the last liquid stool and never beyond 48 consecutive hours at these doses because of ileus risk. The patient-facing page should direct to an individually prescribed local oncology plan rather than print an unsupervised automatic prescription. Assess infectious causes, fever, blood, severe pain and dehydration promptly.
Scan timing is Consultant-plan-specific; no universal three-month CT or tumour-marker schedule is specified in NCCP00794. Routine ECG/echo/DXA should not be added merely to fill a timeline.
Software source reconciliation and 143 scenario/structure checks do not constitute independent Consultant or oncology-pharmacy validation.

Blood-count rules differ between Day 1 and Day 8. Known reduced UGT1A1 activity may increase side effects, but routine genotype testing is not required by the EU product information. Important differences between the NCCP and current EU dose-modification wording are flagged for Consultant and oncology-pharmacy review; patients should never change the dose themselves.

Discuss fertility before treatment. Effective contraception is needed during treatment and for six months after the final dose for women who could become pregnant, and for three months for male patients with female partners who could become pregnant. Do not breastfeed during treatment; the EU product information also advises against breastfeeding for one month after the last dose.
An ECG is used when clinically indicated. Sacituzumab alone does not require a routine echocardiogram schedule. Cardiac symptoms or other medicines may change the plan.
A routine DXA scan is not a sacituzumab-specific requirement. Bone health, bone metastases and any bone-strengthening treatment need their own individual plan.

Response assessment in advanced breast cancer is generally every two to four months, adapted to disease dynamics, sites, symptoms and treatment. Less frequent monitoring may suit indolent disease. New symptoms or suspected progression need earlier assessment. The team chooses the imaging method; this is not an automatic three-month CT chest/abdomen/pelvis order.

If informative, particularly when elevated at baseline or disease is not readily measurable, tumour markers may supplement clinical assessment and imaging. A marker rise alone should not trigger a treatment change. There is no universal fixed marker timetable.

patient.title: Tucatinib + capecitabine + trastuzumab

agents.name: Tucatinib
agents.explanation: Tucatinib reduces signalling from the internal part of HER2. It works alongside trastuzumab and capecitabine, which act in different ways. Its tablet schedule continues through the capecitabine break.
agents.watch: Report diarrhoea early, especially with poor intake. Liver tests and a full medicines review are important.
risks: Liver test changes or liver injury

agents.name: Capecitabine
agents.explanation: The body converts capecitabine into fluorouracil, which disrupts DNA and RNA processes needed for cell growth. Tablets are active chemotherapy; taking them at home still requires a clear monitoring and interruption plan.
agents.watch: Stop tablets and contact the team for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth ulcers, hand-foot soreness affecting activities, fever or dehydration. Chest pain needs urgent assessment. Do not restart until instructed.
risks: Severe early toxicity including DPD-related toxicity

agents.name: Trastuzumab
agents.explanation: Trastuzumab binds to the HER2 protein on cells and helps reduce HER2-driven growth and recruit immune activity. HER2 testing identifies the cancers for which this approach is used.
agents.watch: Attend planned echoes. Report breathlessness, ankle swelling, rapid weight gain or infusion symptoms.

clinical.component_rationale: Tucatinib reduces signalling from the internal part of HER2. It works alongside trastuzumab and capecitabine, which act in different ways. Its tablet schedule continues through the capecitabine break. The body converts capecitabine into fluorouracil, which disrupts DNA and RNA processes needed for cell growth. Tablets are active chemotherapy; taking them at home still requires a clear monitoring and interruption plan. Trastuzumab binds to the HER2 protein on cells and helps reduce HER2-driven growth and recruit immune activity. HER2 testing identifies the cancers for which this approach is used.
key_points: Tumour markers, if useful, supplement symptoms and imaging. They must not alone decide whether treatment is working or should change.
Brain metastases were included in HER2CLIMB, but this does not set a universal brain MRI interval. Confirm the individual CNS imaging / radiotherapy plan.
Tucatinib can raise creatinine through transporter effects. Assess true renal function and dehydration before adjusting capecitabine; do not dismiss a rise automatically.
The current NCCP regimen includes an alternative locally approved SC trastuzumab schedule. Record route before applying dose or missed-dose advice.
Capecitabine DPD, renal and diarrhoea rules are not tucatinib rules; do not apply a single blanket percentage reduction to all components.

administration: Tucatinib 300 mg twice daily continuously, approximately 12 hours apart, with or without food; swallow whole.
Capecitabine 1000 mg/m² twice daily Days 1–14, then a 7-day break; take whole with food or within 30 minutes after food.

A missed tucatinib dose is skipped; take the next usual scheduled dose. Do not make up omitted capecitabine doses. Trastuzumab missed doses follow formulation-specific instructions.

rationale.summary: Tucatinib inhibits intracellular HER2 signalling, trastuzumab binds extracellular HER2, and capecitabine supplies fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy. The combination aims to control previously treated HER2-positive advanced disease.
rationale.setting: Adults with HER2-positive locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer after at least two prior anti-HER2 regimens; NCCP00936v1 eligibility includes ECOG 0–1.
rationale.line: After at least two prior anti-HER2 regimens under NCCP; HER2CLIMB required previous trastuzumab, pertuzumab and T-DM1.

alternatives: Other HER2-directed options depend on previous exposure, CNS disease, current evidence, comorbidity and preferences. There is no head-to-head comparison here with T-DXd.
limitations: HER2CLIMB preceded routine T-DXd sequencing; do not claim trial-proven benefit for every modern sequence.
The updated PFS analysis is investigator assessed and descriptive after unblinding/crossover; do not label it the original primary analysis.

The NCCP exclusion wording says known DPD deficiency, while the dose section allows partial deficiency with reduced starting dose. Complete deficiency excludes capecitabine; partial deficiency needs individual review, not a generic percentage.

support.title: Review the full medicine plan
support.text: Dexamethasone 8 mg orally twice daily for 3 days starting the day before docetaxel; at least 3 doses before treatment unless contraindicated. Missed doses require contact; 20 mg IV replacement is consultant-directed. Reconcile the complete steroid plan with the antiemetic plan; do not add duplicate dexamethasone. Low emetic risk: separate prevention/rescue medicines according to the national/local plan. Prophylactic G-CSF may be used after individual risk assessment.

questions.q: What changes between phases?
questions.a: Docetaxel 75 mg/m² by IV infusion on Day 1 every 21 days. Duration depends on the cancer and treatment aim: NSCLC has a source maximum of six cycles; other indications require an explicitly agreed course, including prostate treatment. This differs from the 100 mg/m² card.

questions.q: When are heart checks due?
questions.a: No routine fixed-cycle echo or ECG is mandated for this regimen alone; assess symptoms and individual cardiac risk. Test timing follows the treatment, clinical findings and local pathway.

questions.q: Where do surgery and radiotherapy fit?
questions.a: Surgery and radiation follow your actual cancer-specific treatment plan. This shared taxane card does not impose an adjuvant breast sequence.

questions.q: Do I need routine CT scans or tumour markers?
questions.a: Agree response imaging and any tumour markers for the actual primary cancer, disease sites and treatment aim. The metastatic breast 2–4-month example is not a universal interval for lung, prostate, gastric, ovarian or bladder cancer.

questions.q: Does a port mean a pump at home?
questions.a: No. This regimen has no routine take-home infusion pump. A port is an access device; the team removes the needle after the visit when appropriate and arranges device removal separately.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: Docetaxel may slow or shrink advanced breast cancer and help symptoms. The dose is selected to balance benefit and side effects; results from a different dose or another cancer do not predict your outcome.

evidence.interpretation: The treating team considers the cancer, previous treatment, health and your priorities. Trial averages do not predict an individual outcome.
evidence.limitations: Evidence is specific to the population and schedule studied. Discuss expected benefit, alternatives and uncertainty for your own treatment.

questions.q: Which treatment days and breaks should I expect?
questions.a: Pegylated liposomal doxorubicin on Day 1 every 28 days, typically for six cycles or until progression or unacceptable toxicity. The team confirms the intended duration and reviews benefit.

questions.q: When do I need blood tests, an ECG or echo?
questions.a: FBC, renal and liver profile before starting and before each 28-day cycle. Check mouth soreness, palms / soles and recovery from earlier toxicity before each dose. ECG is part of baseline and regular monitoring. The NCCP source advises frequent ECG monitoring; the team should specify when it is due rather than assuming an arbitrary cycle interval. Baseline echo / MUGA is required. Repeat during treatment as clinically indicated, and before each additional administration that exceeds a lifetime cumulative anthracycline exposure of 450 mg/m². Prior anthracyclines count; this threshold is not an automatic treatment stop.

questions.q: When will we know whether treatment is helping?
questions.a: For metastatic breast cancer, ESMO recommends response evaluation generally every 2–4 months, adjusted to disease, treatment and symptoms. Agree the scan type, due window and result-review appointment; symptoms can prompt earlier assessment. For the other cancer indications on this card, use the cancer-specific monitoring plan; the breast interval is not transferred automatically.

questions.q: Where do surgery or radiotherapy fit?
questions.a: These are advanced-disease regimens. Surgery or radiotherapy is used only for a defined local or symptom-control purpose. The oncology and radiation teams decide whether chemotherapy continues, pauses or precedes radiation; no routine overlap is implied.

questions.q: Do tumour markers replace scans?
questions.a: Tumour markers, when useful for the cancer being treated, supplement clinical assessment and imaging. A marker result alone should not determine treatment failure or a treatment change.

questions.q: Does a port mean a pump at home?
questions.a: No. A port is a route into a vein. Staff disconnect the infusion and remove the port needle after the visit when appropriate; removal of the implanted device is a separate planned procedure.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: In a study in metastatic breast cancer, this liposomal formulation controlled cancer about as well as conventional doxorubicin and caused fewer heart problems, but more hand–foot and mouth problems. It can still affect the heart, and personal benefit is uncertain.
evidence.population: NCCP 00205 a: metastatic breast cancer. Other source indications are separate; do not apply breast efficacy results to them.
evidence.interpretation: The treating team considers the cancer, previous treatment, health and your priorities. Trial averages do not predict an individual outcome.
evidence.limitations: Evidence is specific to the population and schedule studied. Discuss expected benefit, alternatives and uncertainty for your own treatment.

items.title: Evidence limits
items.text: Comparable progression-free survival with less cardiotoxicity for PLD, while hand-foot syndrome and oral toxicity were more frequent. Overall survival was similar. Breast-trial findings do not establish efficacy in every NCCP 00205 cross-cancer indication. Normal cardiac function was required in this trial; lower cardiotoxicity does not mean cardiac safety in established heart disease or removal of monitoring. Do not interchange pegylated liposomal, non-pegylated liposomal and conventional doxorubicin.

patient.title: Weekly paclitaxel

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Cells use tiny structures called microtubules to separate their chromosomes when dividing. Paclitaxel stabilises these structures so they cannot rearrange normally, interrupting cell division. It can also affect nerves and other healthy tissues.
agents.watch: Report tingling or numbness before the next weekly dose, especially if it affects walking or hand use. Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, chest or throat tightness, itching, dizziness or breathing changes during infusion.
risks: Sensory or motor neuropathy, potentially persistent
Hair loss and nail / skin changes
Rare serious lung or cardiac effects

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

patient.urgent_extra: New chest pain, breathing difficulty, severe diarrhoea, inability to drink, reduced urine, uncontrolled bleeding or a rapidly worsening symptom needs prompt assessment.

chapters.title: Which cancer setting does this page cover?
chapters.intro: The regimen number matters as well as the drug name.

items.title: Advanced breast cancer
items.text: The NCCP indication concerns metastatic breast cancer after unsuitable or unsuccessful anthracycline-based treatment. Tumour biology and previous treatments influence options. This page does not describe every early-breast-cancer paclitaxel regimen.

items.title: Ovarian, small-cell lung and bladder cancer
items.text: These are specific later-line settings in this shared protocol. Evidence is less robust than for the breast-cancer weekly comparison. Ask about current alternatives and the implications of use outside the licensed indication where applicable.

items.title: Paclitaxel formulations and combinations
items.text: Conventional paclitaxel and nab-paclitaxel have different formulations and administration requirements. This is a single-agent paclitaxel guide. If another anti-cancer medicine is added, obtain the matching combination guide.

items.title: What matters to you?
items.text: Discuss symptom control, time in hospital, hair loss, neuropathy risk and the activities you most want to preserve. Your priorities can change. Supportive care is available alongside active treatment.

chapters.title: Before each weekly visit
chapters.intro: Use the time between appointments to make review more informative.

items.title: Write down change from your baseline
items.text: Record tingling, numbness, pain, balance, bowel symptoms and fatigue. Tell the team about fever or illness when it occurs; the record is not a reason to wait.

items.title: Check medicines and transport
items.text: Know whether premedication is taken at home or given in hospital. Bring your medicine list and tell the team about a previous infusion reaction. Sedating antihistamines can affect driving.

items.title: Know the agreed schedule
items.text: Check the planned treatment days and blood-test arrangements. A three-visit and four-visit schedule must be distinguished in your own prescription. The number of visits may change after clinical review.

chapters.title: What the checks are for
chapters.intro: Symptoms, blood results and the treatment aim answer different questions.

items.title: Blood counts
items.text: Neutrophils protect against infection, haemoglobin carries oxygen and platelets help clotting. A normal previous result or feeling well does not prove the current counts are safe. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate advice.

items.title: Kidney and liver function
items.text: Organ function can change drug exposure. Vomiting or diarrhoea can cause dehydration and worsen kidney function. Report reduced urine, poor intake, jaundice and new medicines. The clinical assessment combines results with symptoms.

items.title: Describe symptoms in practical terms
items.text: Tell the team about the worst symptoms since the last visit, even if improved today. Examples include extra stools above your usual pattern, whether mouth pain affects drinking, and whether numbness affects buttons or balance.

items.title: Assessing cancer control
items.text: The review plan may use scans, symptoms and ability to manage daily life. Stable disease can be worthwhile. Ask what benefit would justify continuing and what alternatives would be considered if treatment stops helping.

chapters.title: What to watch for
chapters.intro: Some effects appear early; others build over repeated doses.

items.title: Neuropathy and lasting effects
items.text: Paclitaxel can affect sensation and sometimes strength. Report numbness, burning pain, weakness or difficulty with everyday tasks before the next dose. Symptoms may take time to improve and can persist after treatment.

items.title: Aches and fatigue
items.text: Muscle or joint pain can occur after treatment. Use the agreed analgesia plan and describe how pain affects sleep and function. New extreme weakness, fainting or breathlessness should be assessed rather than attributed automatically to treatment.

items.title: Hair, skin and nails
items.text: Hair loss is common with paclitaxel; it may include body hair. Nail changes and skin symptoms can occur. Ask about practical support and report painful, infected or rapidly worsening changes.

items.title: Mouth, bowels and infection
items.text: Gentle mouth care and early reporting help when soreness affects eating. Report persistent diarrhoea or vomiting. Low blood counts can make infection dangerous; a normal temperature does not make sudden illness safe.

items.title: Infusion and breathing symptoms
items.text: Reactions can occur during infusion despite premedication. Tell the nurse immediately. New cough or breathlessness after leaving also needs assessment; the cause may be infection, a clot, treatment or cancer.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: Plan around the activities and people that matter to you.

items.title: Food, drink and practical help
items.text: Use foods and drinks you can manage. Tell the team about weight loss, poor intake or difficulty shopping and cooking; ask for dietitian or practical support. A fixed daily fluid target is not appropriate for everyone, particularly with heart or kidney problems.

items.title: Activity, rest and driving
items.text: Balance rest with manageable activity. Record what fatigue stops you doing. Do not drive when dizzy, unwell or affected by sedating medicines. Ask about work adjustments and transport for treatment days.

items.title: Medicines, vaccines and supplements
items.text: Bring a complete medicine list, including over-the-counter products and supplements. Ask the oncology pharmacist before changes. Discuss vaccination timing. Do not stop prescribed long-term medicines on your own.

items.title: Fertility, contraception and breastfeeding
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment when relevant. Ask for a written contraception and breastfeeding plan covering each medicine and the period after treatment. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy.

items.title: Support for you and your family
items.text: Ask about psycho-oncology, social work, counselling and symptom support. Take information in manageable amounts. A family member or trusted person can help record questions if you wish. Discuss how treatment fits your priorities.

chapters.title: Useful treatment terms
chapters.intro: Short explanations for the clinic conversation.

items.title: Taxane and microtubule
items.text: A taxane is a chemotherapy drug family. Microtubules are small cell structures involved in division and other functions. Effects on these structures help explain both anti-cancer activity and nerve toxicity.

items.title: Premedication and neuropathy
items.text: Premedication is medicine given before an infusion to reduce reactions. Neuropathy means nerve dysfunction. These are separate issues and both need review during weekly therapy.

chapters.title: Benefit, course and continuing checks
chapters.intro: Weekly paclitaxel can shrink or slow metastatic breast cancer. In a breast cancer study it produced more tumour responses than treatment given less often, but more severe nerve symptoms. Some trial participants also received trastuzumab, so the result does not predict every monotherapy outcome.

items.title: Before and during treatment
items.text: FBC, renal and liver profile before each treatment, including each weekly dose. Review neuropathy, function, infusion reactions and symptoms before every administration.

items.title: Heart checks and the full course
items.text: Review cardiac symptoms and monitor observations during infusion. No fixed routine echo schedule is imposed for this paclitaxel monotherapy; significant conduction abnormalities require cardiac monitoring. Default Days 1, 8, 15 and 22 every 28 days. The consultant may choose Days 1, 8 and 15 only; confirm the selected plan. Each dose needs its own review.

patient.purpose: This weekly paclitaxel protocol is used in specified advanced breast, ovarian, small-cell lung and bladder-cancer settings. The aim is usually disease control and symptom relief. Evidence and alternatives differ between cancers; confirm the indication with your oncologist.

timeline.label: Blood counts / energy
timeline.text: Review before each dose; report illness any day

day_groups.title: First visit of this cycle
day_groups.body: Review symptoms, blood results and premedication before the infusion. Tell the nurse straight away about itching, flushing, throat or chest tightness, back pain, dizziness or breathing change.
day_groups.action: Check transport if premedication makes you drowsy and confirm the next weekly visit.

day_groups.title: Between weekly doses
day_groups.body: Aches, fatigue, nausea or bowel symptoms may occur. Tingling may be mild at first but matters before the next dose. Record what symptoms stop you doing.
day_groups.action: Contact the team for new or worsening numbness, balance trouble, marked weakness or uncontrolled symptoms. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate contact.

day_groups.title: Second weekly review
day_groups.body: This dose requires its own symptom and blood-test review. Describe the worst symptoms since the previous visit, not only how you feel today.
day_groups.action: Report sensory changes before the infusion and confirm your premedication instructions.

day_groups.title: Keep tracking function
day_groups.body: Repeated treatment can increase nerve symptoms and fatigue. Check practical tasks such as buttons, writing and walking. Use the symptom passport to show changes.
day_groups.action: Seek early advice rather than waiting until numbness is severe.

day_groups.title: Third weekly review
day_groups.body: The team decides whether treatment can proceed using the current assessment.
day_groups.action: Confirm whether Day 22 is planned for you; do not infer this from a different person’s calendar.

day_groups.title: After the third visit
day_groups.body: Symptoms may settle or continue. An interval between appointments does not rule out infection or a treatment complication.
day_groups.action: Use the urgent contact plan if unwell and bring your record to the next review.

day_groups.title: Day 22: follow the prescribed schedule
day_groups.body: A fourth dose is part of the four-visit plan. In the consultant-selected three-visit plan there is no Day 22 infusion. The calendar here is educational.
day_groups.action: Use your confirmed appointment and prescription; call if the schedule is unclear.

day_groups.title: Complete the cycle record
day_groups.body: Record symptoms and functional changes, including those that improve before the next appointment. Treatment continuation depends on benefit, toxicity and your priorities.
day_groups.action: Check the next cycle date and review plan. Do not treat a gap in visits as a guarantee of recovery.

support.title: Premedication for infusion reactions
support.text: Steroid and antihistamine premedication reduce the chance or severity of reactions. The team may adjust premedication after tolerated doses. Do not omit or change it yourself; tell the nurse about missed doses.

support.title: Aches, nausea and bowel support
support.text: Agree a pain-relief and anti-sickness plan. Ask before taking new medicines. Uncontrolled pain or poor intake needs review. Some supportive medicines cause constipation or drowsiness.

support.title: Nerve symptoms and fall prevention
support.text: Use secure footwear and take care with balance, hot surfaces and sharp objects if sensation is reduced. Tell the team early about functional changes; persistent neuropathy may influence dosing.

support.title: Hair, nails and skin
support.text: Ask about hair-loss support and whether scalp cooling is appropriate and available. Protect sensitive nails and skin. Report painful nail changes, spreading rash, blistering or infection.

support.title: Review the full medicine plan
support.text: First-dose NCCP suggested premedication: dexamethasone 8 mg IV, chlorphenamine 10 mg IV and famotidine 20 mg IV 30 minutes before paclitaxel. From Day 8, dexamethasone may be omitted in the source suggested table; add or modify for increased risk or previous reaction under consultant guidance. Famotidine omission is also a consultant/local-policy decision requiring close observation. The conventional paclitaxel product information has a different generic premedication regimen. Reconcile the exact product, weekly NCCP pathway and local policy; never self-omit premedication. Low emetic risk; keep the antiemetic plan separate from reaction premedication. Consider analgesia for myalgia/arthralgia and early action on neuropathy.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: Weekly paclitaxel can shrink or slow metastatic breast cancer. In a breast cancer study it produced more tumour responses than treatment given less often, but more severe nerve symptoms. Some trial participants also received trastuzumab, so the result does not predict every monotherapy outcome.
evidence.population: NCCP 00226 a: metastatic breast carcinoma after failure of, or when unsuitable for, standard anthracycline-containing therapy. Other source cancers retain separate evidence and eligibility.
evidence.interpretation: The treating team considers the cancer, previous treatment, health and your priorities. Trial averages do not predict an individual outcome.
evidence.limitations: Evidence is specific to the population and schedule studied. Discuss expected benefit, alternatives and uncertainty for your own treatment.

chronology_notes.title: Day 22
chronology_notes.text: The fourth visit applies only to the four-visit plan. Some patients are prescribed Days 1, 8 and 15; follow your confirmed schedule.

chronology_notes.title: Nerves and aches
chronology_notes.text: Aches can follow treatment; numbness, tingling and fatigue may persist or accumulate. Describe changes before the next dose.

chronology_notes.title: Blood counts
chronology_notes.text: A gap between visits does not exclude infection or another treatment complication. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate contact.

questions.q: Which treatment days and breaks should I expect?
questions.a: Eribulin on Days 1 and 8 of each 21-day cycle. Day 15 is a planned treatment-free week. Treatment continues while beneficial and tolerated.

questions.q: When do I need blood tests, an ECG or echo?
questions.a: FBC, renal and liver profile before starting and at the start of each cycle. The EMA product information specifies FBC before every dose, including Day 8; additional renal / liver tests follow clinical need. ECG before starting and during treatment when there is cardiac disease, a slow / abnormal rhythm, QT-prolonging medicines or electrolyte disturbance. Correct low potassium, calcium or magnesium before treatment; repeat monitoring follows risk and findings. No fixed routine echo interval is specified for eribulin alone. Cardiac symptoms or risk prompt individual assessment. If trastuzumab is separately prescribed, use its own cardiac-monitoring plan.

questions.q: When will we know whether treatment is helping?
questions.a: For metastatic breast cancer, ESMO recommends response evaluation generally every 2–4 months, adjusted to disease, treatment and symptoms. Agree the scan type, due window and result-review appointment; symptoms can prompt earlier assessment. For the other cancer indications on this card, use the cancer-specific monitoring plan; the breast interval is not transferred automatically.

questions.q: Where do surgery or radiotherapy fit?
questions.a: These are advanced-disease regimens. Surgery or radiotherapy is used only for a defined local or symptom-control purpose. The oncology and radiation teams decide whether chemotherapy continues, pauses or precedes radiation; no routine overlap is implied.

questions.q: Do tumour markers replace scans?
questions.a: Tumour markers, when useful for the cancer being treated, supplement clinical assessment and imaging. A marker result alone should not determine treatment failure or a treatment change.

questions.q: Does a port mean a pump at home?
questions.a: No. A port is a route into a vein. Staff disconnect the infusion and remove the port needle after the visit when appropriate; removal of the implanted device is a separate planned procedure.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: In heavily pretreated advanced breast cancer, eribulin helped people live longer on average than the comparison treatments chosen by their doctors. This does not predict an individual result or establish the same benefit in every treatment line or another cancer.
evidence.population: NCCP 00228 a: locally advanced/metastatic breast cancer progressing after at least one chemotherapy regimen for advanced disease; prior anthracycline and taxane unless unsuitable. Liposarcoma is a separate source indication.
evidence.interpretation: The treating team considers the cancer, previous treatment, health and your priorities. Trial averages do not predict an individual outcome.
evidence.limitations: Evidence is specific to the population and schedule studied. Discuss expected benefit, alternatives and uncertainty for your own treatment.

items.title: Evidence limits
items.text: In heavily pretreated advanced breast cancer, eribulin helped people live longer on average than the comparison treatments chosen by their doctors. This does not predict an individual result or establish the same benefit in every treatment line or another cancer. EU dose is 1.23 mg/m² eribulin base; 1.4 mg/m² mesylate in trial reports is the equivalent amount, not an alternative numeric prescription. Day 8 may be delayed or omitted after review.

items.title: Eribulin versus dacarbazine: advanced liposarcoma evidence
items.text: 452 adults with advanced liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma after at least two systemic regimens including anthracycline, using Days 1 and 8 every 21 days. Separate sarcoma trial and its liposarcoma subgroup support the liposarcoma indication; breast-trial benefit figures do not apply. The licensed liposarcoma indication must not be expanded to all sarcomas because the parent trial also enrolled leiomyosarcoma. Use current NCCP eligibility and EMA indication wording. Do not apply breast imaging or CA 15-3/CEA pathways to liposarcoma.

agents.name: Olaparib (Lynparza)
agents.mechanism: Disrupts DNA repair in susceptible cancer cells
visual: DNA damage accumulates in cancer cells
agents.explanation: BRCA1 and BRCA2 help cells repair breaks in DNA. Some cancers with these changes rely more heavily on other repair routes. Olaparib inhibits PARP activity and traps PARP on DNA, making it harder for those cancer cells to survive DNA damage. Normal blood-forming cells can also be affected, which is why regular blood counts matter.
agents.watch: Keep the four-weekly blood reviews and report persistent nausea, marked fatigue, infections, bleeding or new respiratory symptoms. Severe blood abnormalities need review even if you feel well.
risks: Nausea, vomiting, reduced appetite and indigestion
Low neutrophils or platelets, with infection or bleeding risk
Uncommon but serious pneumonitis or drug-induced liver injury
Rare serious marrow disorders, including MDS/AML
Venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism; risk differs by treatment setting
Fetal harm; contraception and breastfeeding restrictions

sections.title: After chemotherapy and local treatment
sections.text: Olaparib follows the chemotherapy and local-treatment plan. In OlympiA, surgery and any indicated radiotherapy were completed before olaparib, with at least a two-week gap after local treatment. NCCP advises starting ideally within twelve weeks of the last surgery, chemotherapy or radiation; your team sets the start.

sections.title: Endocrine therapy may overlap
sections.text: For hormone receptor-positive disease, the prescribed hormone treatment can continue alongside olaparib and often continues after the one-year olaparib course. Its injections, tablets and bone checks keep their own schedule.

sections.title: A daily routine at home
sections.text: Choose consistent morning and evening times and check the strength and number of tablets on each new prescription. Keep a sufficient supply before weekends or holidays. No infusion pump or port is needed for olaparib itself.

sections.title: If treatment is paused
sections.text: The oncology team decides when and at what dose to restart after blood recovery or symptom improvement. Do not calculate a catch-up dose or restart automatically because a calendar month has passed.

sections.title: After the planned year
sections.text: Agree the stop date and ongoing breast follow-up. Endocrine treatment and breast surveillance may continue. Report persistent unexplained fatigue, infections, bruising or breathlessness even after olaparib finishes.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: In people with the high-risk inherited BRCA-associated breast cancer studied, one year of olaparib reduced invasive recurrence and improved survival. Longer follow-up shows that the benefit persists after treatment ends. Eligibility is specific, and benefit for an individual remains uncertain.
evidence.population: NCCP 00588 h only: germline pathogenic BRCA1/2-associated HER2-negative high-risk early breast cancer after neoadjuvant/adjuvant chemotherapy. Do not route other 00588 indications into this breast suite.
evidence.interpretation: The treating team considers the cancer, previous treatment, health and your priorities. Trial averages do not predict an individual outcome.
evidence.limitations: Evidence is specific to the population and schedule studied. Discuss expected benefit, alternatives and uncertainty for your own treatment.

patient.teachback: Which medicine is taken or given when, what checks are expected next, and which symptoms mean you should call today?
patient.consent_support: This patient suite is only for breast adjuvant indication 00588 h. Kidney/liver impairment, previous dose reductions and interacting medicines can change the dose. New blood abnormalities can occasionally signal a serious marrow problem and must be investigated. Olaparib can harm an unborn baby. Discuss effective contraception before treatment; EMA recommends two reliable complementary methods for women during treatment and for six months afterwards. Men and their partners need contraception during treatment and for three months afterwards. Do not breastfeed during treatment or for one month after the last dose.

chapters.title: The exact treatment being discussed
chapters.intro: Reduce the chance of invasive recurrence after standard chemotherapy and local treatment. It may be taken alongside prescribed endocrine therapy for hormone receptor-positive disease.

items.title: Who this covers
items.text: Adults with a confirmed pathogenic germline BRCA1/2 mutation, HER2-negative high-risk early breast cancer and previous neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy. The high-risk definition depends on hormone receptors, prior chemotherapy setting, surgical pathology and, for one pathway, CPS+EG score.

items.title: Dose and administration
items.text: Usually 300 mg twice daily; follow the individual prescription. Swallow tablets whole with water, with or without food. Do not chew, crush, dissolve or divide them. If a dose is missed, take the next normal dose at its usual time; do not double it. Check tablet strength after any dose change.

items.title: Duration and decisions
items.text: For breast indication 00588 h: up to one year, or earlier if the cancer recurs or side effects make treatment unsuitable. This is different from olaparib durations in ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancer.

items.title: Individual safety and source differences
items.text: This patient suite is only for breast adjuvant indication 00588 h. Kidney/liver impairment, previous dose reductions and interacting medicines can change the dose. New blood abnormalities can occasionally signal a serious marrow problem and must be investigated.

chapters.title: Checks throughout treatment
chapters.intro: Blood tests assess treatment safety. Scans assess disease or investigate symptoms. Echo and ECG answer different questions.

items.title: Before treatment
items.text: Confirm the germline BRCA result and breast eligibility. Review blood count, kidney and liver tests, recovery from previous treatment, medicines and supplements, and pregnancy testing where relevant. Confirm the surgery/radiotherapy sequence and the planned start.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: NCCP specifies FBC, kidney and liver tests every four weeks for the first twelve months. Reviews also assess nausea, appetite, energy, bruising, infections and breathing symptoms. Extra tests or an interruption may be needed if results or symptoms change.

items.title: Heart checks
items.text: Olaparib alone has no routine ECG or echo surveillance timetable in this NCCP regimen. Heart checks may still be needed because of previous anthracycline/HER2 treatment, existing disease or new symptoms.

items.title: Bone health
items.text: There is no olaparib-specific DXA schedule. If an aromatase inhibitor or ovarian suppression is also prescribed, retain that treatment’s separate bone-density and bone-health plan.

chapters.title: Your wider treatment plan
chapters.intro: Additional treatments depend on the confirmed setting and indication.

items.title: Early-breast follow-up
items.text: After early breast cancer treatment, annual mammography is generally used for remaining breast tissue: both breasts after conservation, or the opposite breast after unilateral mastectomy. Routine mammography of the mastectomy side is not required. Routine CT, bone scans and tumour markers are not recommended solely to look for recurrence in an asymptomatic person. Safety blood tests for ongoing olaparib are a separate requirement. New symptoms need assessment between appointments.

items.title: Tumour markers
items.text: No routine tumour-marker surveillance for asymptomatic early breast cancer.

items.title: Pregnancy, fertility and contraception
items.text: Olaparib can harm an unborn baby. Discuss effective contraception before treatment; EMA recommends two reliable complementary methods for women during treatment and for six months afterwards. Men and their partners need contraception during treatment and for three months afterwards. Do not breastfeed during treatment or for one month after the last dose.

chapters.title: Evidence depends on the population
chapters.intro: Different studies answer different questions; do not compare their results as if populations and follow-up were identical.

items.title: OlympiA: four-year survival analysis
items.text: The earlier survival update showed that the benefit extended beyond preventing invasive recurrence. These results apply to the selected high-risk inherited BRCA-associated early breast population, not every HER2-negative breast cancer.

items.title: OlympiA: sustained benefit at six years
items.text: Longer follow-up confirms that reductions in invasive recurrence and improvements in survival persist after the planned year of treatment. This is follow-up after one year of olaparib, not a longer prescribed course; rare late marrow effects still need attention.

chapters.title: Benefit, course and continuing checks
chapters.intro: In people with the high-risk inherited BRCA-associated breast cancer studied, one year of olaparib reduced invasive recurrence and improved survival. Longer follow-up shows that the benefit persists after treatment ends. Eligibility is specific, and benefit for an individual remains uncertain.

items.title: Before and during treatment

items.title: Heart checks and the full course
items.text: No routine olaparib-specific ECG, echo or DXA; follow separate previous/ongoing treatment risks. Breast surveillance continues after olaparib, without automatic asymptomatic CT or tumour-marker scheduling. High risk:TNBC residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy or node-positive/≥2 cm after adjuvant chemotherapy; HR-positive disease requires residual disease with CPS+EG≥3 after neoadjuvant therapy or≥4 positive nodes after adjuvant chemotherapy. Ideally start within 12 weeks of the last surgery, chemotherapy or radiation.

questions.q: When do I take or receive treatment?
questions.a: Take olaparib tablets morning and evening every day. There is no planned week off. Blood-review appointments are usually every four weeks during this one-year breast course. Swallow tablets whole with water, with or without food. Do not chew, crush, dissolve or divide them. If a dose is missed, take the next normal dose at its usual time; do not double it. Check tablet strength after any dose change.

questions.q: When are bloods, ECGs or echoes needed?
questions.a: Confirm the germline BRCA result and breast eligibility. Review blood count, kidney and liver tests, recovery from previous treatment, medicines and supplements, and pregnancy testing where relevant. Confirm the surgery/radiotherapy sequence and the planned start. NCCP specifies FBC, kidney and liver tests every four weeks for the first twelve months. Reviews also assess nausea, appetite, energy, bruising, infections and breathing symptoms. Extra tests or an interruption may be needed if results or symptoms change. Olaparib alone has no routine ECG or echo surveillance timetable in this NCCP regimen. Heart checks may still be needed because of previous anthracycline/HER2 treatment, existing disease or new symptoms.

questions.q: Which scans apply to me?
questions.a: After early breast cancer treatment, annual mammography is generally used for remaining breast tissue: both breasts after conservation, or the opposite breast after unilateral mastectomy. Routine mammography of the mastectomy side is not required. Routine CT, bone scans and tumour markers are not recommended solely to look for recurrence in an asymptomatic person. Safety blood tests for ongoing olaparib are a separate requirement. New symptoms need assessment between appointments.

questions.q: How long will treatment continue?
questions.a: For breast indication 00588 h: up to one year, or earlier if the cancer recurs or side effects make treatment unsuitable. This is different from olaparib durations in ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancer.

questions.q: What should make me call today?
questions.a: Contact the oncology team urgently for fever or feeling acutely unwell, unusual bleeding, new or worsening breathlessness/cough, severe weakness, persistent vomiting or inability to drink. Chest pain, severe breathing difficulty or collapse require emergency help.

questions.q: What is my bone-health plan?
questions.a: There is no olaparib-specific DXA schedule. If an aromatase inhibitor or ovarian suppression is also prescribed, retain that treatment’s separate bone-density and bone-health plan.

rationale.summary: Olaparib exploits impaired homologous-recombination repair in BRCA-associated cancer. A one-year adjuvant course reduces invasive recurrence and improves survival in selected high-risk HER2-negative early breast disease after chemotherapy and local therapy.
rationale.setting: NCCP 00588 h only: germline pathogenic BRCA1/2-associated HER2-negative high-risk early breast cancer after neoadjuvant/adjuvant chemotherapy. Do not route other 00588 indications into this breast suite.

clinical.component_rationale: Olaparib (Lynparza): BRCA1 and BRCA2 help cells repair breaks in DNA. Some cancers with these changes rely more heavily on other repair routes. Olaparib inhibits PARP activity and traps PARP on DNA, making it harder for those cancer cells to survive DNA damage. Normal blood-forming cells can also be affected, which is why regular blood counts matter.

endpoints.result_text: Olaparib 79.6% versus placebo 70.3%; HR 0.65 (95% CI 0.53–0.78); reported difference 9.4 percentage points (95% CI 5.1–12.7).

evidence.qualitative_result: Longer follow-up confirms sustained invasive disease-free and overall-survival benefit from one year of adjuvant olaparib.
limitations: Do not extend to BRCA variants of uncertain significance, all HER2-negative cancers, concurrent radiation or the other 00588 organ-specific indications. This update does not lengthen the one-year breast course.
evidence.harms: Blood toxicity and gastrointestinal symptoms require continuing review. MDS/AML remained uncommon in the six-year report (0.4% olaparib, 0.7% placebo); rare late toxicity still requires surveillance.

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Cells use tiny structures called microtubules to separate their chromosomes when dividing. Paclitaxel stabilises these structures so they cannot rearrange normally, interrupting cell division. It can also affect nerves and other healthy tissues.
agents.watch: Report tingling or numbness before the next dose, especially if it affects walking or hand use. Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, chest or throat tightness, itching, dizziness or breathing changes during infusion.

support.title: Review the full medicine plan
support.text: First-dose NCCP suggested premedication: dexamethasone 8 mg IV, chlorphenamine 10 mg IV and famotidine 20 mg IV 30 minutes before paclitaxel. From Day 8, dexamethasone may be omitted in the source suggested table; add or modify for increased risk or previous reaction under consultant guidance. Famotidine omission is also a consultant/local-policy decision requiring close observation. The conventional paclitaxel product information has a different generic premedication regimen. Reconcile the exact product, weekly NCCP pathway and local policy; never self-omit premedication. Low emetic risk; keep the antiemetic plan separate from reaction premedication. Consider analgesia for myalgia/arthralgia and early action on neuropathy.

questions.a: Surgery and radiation follow your actual cancer-specific treatment plan. This shared taxane card does not impose an adjuvant breast sequence.

questions.q: Do I need routine CT scans or tumour markers?

questions.q: Does a port mean a pump at home?
questions.a: No. This regimen has no routine take-home infusion pump. A port is an access device; the team removes the needle after the visit when appropriate and arranges device removal separately.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: Paclitaxel may slow or shrink metastatic breast cancer and help symptoms. This prescribed pattern includes a week without paclitaxel. There is no verified numerical survival estimate for this exact schedule in this review; results from a different weekly pattern do not predict your outcome.

evidence.interpretation: The treating team considers the cancer, previous treatment, health and your priorities. Trial averages do not predict an individual outcome.
evidence.limitations: Evidence is specific to the population and schedule studied. Discuss expected benefit, alternatives and uncertainty for your own treatment.

steps.title: Plan venous access
steps.text: A cannula, PICC or implanted port may be used. If a port is chosen, a trained team inserts it in a separate procedure with local anaesthetic and sometimes sedation; the team explains fasting, blood-thinner and wound instructions.

steps.title: Infusion day
steps.text: Staff check the line, give prescribed premedicines and treatment, and observe for reactions. Tell them immediately about burning, pain, rash or breathlessness.

steps.title: Home and next review
steps.text: This regimen does not routinely need a take-home infusion pump. Staff disconnect the infusion; a port is de-accessed when appropriate. Keep line-care and next-visit instructions.

details.title: Port insertion and removal
details.text: The line team explains placement, dressing care and when normal activities can resume. A port is accessed with a special needle during treatment. Removal of the implanted device is a separate planned procedure when no longer needed; do not remove or adjust it yourself.

details.title: PICC care and urgent line symptoms
details.text: A PICC usually needs regular dressing and flushing appointments even between treatments. Fever, redness, swelling, pain, leakage or damage requires prompt advice. Your hospital supplies the exact care instructions.

details.title: Visit time and transport
details.text: First visits can take longer because of loading doses, premedicines and observation. Ask the unit about expected time, transport and any escort needed after sedation or line insertion.

details.title: Phase-specific visit pattern

patient.title: Weekly cetuximab

agents.name: Cetuximab
agents.mechanism: Blocks growth messages at the cell surface
agents.explanation: Cetuximab attaches to EGFR on the outside of cells and blocks growth messages. In bowel cancer, a validated RAS wild-type result helps identify whether this approach is suitable. In head-and-neck cancer, weekly cetuximab may be combined with radiotherapy under a separate treatment plan. Healthy skin also uses EGFR, so skin and nail effects need early care.
agents.watch: Report rash or sore nails early. Tell the nurse immediately about infusion symptoms. Eye pain, new breathing problems or severe diarrhoea need prompt advice. Blood tests check minerals during treatment and for two months afterwards.
risks: Rash, dry skin, cracks and sore nails
Infusion reaction; rare serious lung or skin effects

questions.q: How is my treatment chosen?
questions.a: Cetuximab alone is an option for RAS wild-type bowel cancer that has spread after oxaliplatin and irinotecan have failed, when irinotecan cannot be tolerated. A separate indication combines weekly cetuximab with radiotherapy for locally advanced head-and-neck cancer; the radiation team confirms suitability, including the current NCCP catalogue criteria. Your team explains the aim, alternatives and how benefit will be reviewed.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates to understand the cycle?
questions.a: No. The graph explains a general pattern. Your hospital arranges appointments; the guide and its safety information are available without entering anything.

questions.q: Will I have a pump at home?
questions.a: There is no home fluorouracil pump in this regimen. Your team chooses a cannula or central line based on your veins and wider treatment plan.

questions.q: What happens if a dose is delayed?
questions.a: The team checks the cause and may delay, reduce, change or stop one medicine. Ask which component changes and when you should next attend; do not restart yourself.

questions.q: How will I know whether it is helping?
questions.a: Scans, symptoms and clinical review assess benefit. A rash, side effect or good day alone cannot show whether the cancer is responding.

questions.q: What about radiotherapy?
questions.a: For the head-and-neck indication, cetuximab starts one week before radiation and continues weekly alongside it. The graphic below shows the relationship. Colorectal cetuximab alone does not include a routine radiation course.

questions.q: What about fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding?
questions.a: Discuss fertility preservation and reproductive plans before treatment. Ask for the contraception and breastfeeding instructions for every medicine; the whole regimen may require longer precautions than one medicine alone.

questions.q: Why is RAS testing mentioned?
questions.a: RAS testing selects cetuximab treatment in colorectal cancer. It is not the selection test for the separate head-and-neck radiotherapy indication. Confirm the cancer-specific plan with your team.

questions.q: Which checks continue when treatment changes or finishes?
questions.a: Monthly electrolytes, magnesium and calcium for two months after the last cetuximab dose; assign responsibility before treatment ends. Response assessment follows the consultant plan; head/neck radiation follow-up is coordinated separately.

items.title: A plan that can change
items.text: Ask whether the aim is to reduce recurrence risk, control cancer, relieve symptoms or support a local treatment. Your preferences and priorities matter.

items.title: Separate head-and-neck evidence
items.text: A randomised trial compared radiotherapy plus weekly cetuximab with radiotherapy alone and found improved local control and survival. It did not compare cetuximab with cisplatin; it cannot establish that cetuximab is equivalent to cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy.
