patient.title: Fortnightly cetuximab + irinotecan

agents.name: Cetuximab
agents.mechanism: Blocks growth messages at the cell surface
agents.explanation: Cetuximab attaches to EGFR on the outside of cells and blocks some growth messages. In this bowel-cancer plan, validated extended RAS testing helps identify whether treatment is suitable. Healthy skin also uses EGFR, so skin and nail effects need early care.
agents.watch: Report rash or sore nails early. Tell the nurse immediately about infusion symptoms. Eye pain, new breathing problems or severe diarrhoea need prompt advice. Blood tests check minerals during treatment and for two months afterwards.
risks: Rash, dry skin, cracks and sore nails
Infusion reaction; rare serious lung or skin effects

agents.name: Irinotecan
agents.explanation: The body converts irinotecan into SN-38. This traps an enzyme called topoisomerase I while DNA is being copied, causing damage that can stop cancer cells dividing. Normal bowel and blood-forming cells can also be affected.
agents.watch: Tell the nurse immediately about cramps, sweating or diarrhoea during the infusion. Diarrhoea starting later needs the separate written treatment and contact plan.
risks: Rare serious lung or allergic reactions

questions.q: How is my treatment chosen?
questions.a: This combination is used for RAS wild-type bowel cancer that has spread. This NCCP pathway is a second-line option after oxaliplatin-based treatment has failed or cannot be used. Your team explains the aim, alternatives and how benefit will be reviewed.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates to understand the cycle?
questions.a: No. The graph explains a general pattern. Your hospital arranges appointments; the guide and its safety information are available without entering anything.

questions.q: Will I have a pump at home?
questions.a: There is no home fluorouracil pump in this regimen. Your team chooses a cannula or central line based on your veins and wider treatment plan.

questions.q: What happens if a dose is delayed?
questions.a: The team checks the cause and may delay, reduce, change or stop one medicine. Ask which component changes and when you should next attend; do not restart yourself.

questions.q: How will I know whether it is helping?
questions.a: Scans, symptoms and clinical review assess benefit. A rash, side effect or good day alone cannot show whether the cancer is responding.

questions.q: What about radiotherapy?
questions.a: This NCCP regimen does not contain a routine radiotherapy course. If radiation is recommended separately, ask whether it is before, during or after these medicines.

questions.q: What about fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding?
questions.a: Discuss fertility preservation and reproductive plans before treatment. Ask for the contraception and breastfeeding instructions for every medicine; the whole regimen may require longer precautions than one medicine alone.

questions.q: Why is RAS testing mentioned?
questions.a: RAS testing selects cetuximab treatment in colorectal cancer. It is not the selection test for the separate head-and-neck radiotherapy indication. Confirm the cancer-specific plan with your team.

patient.phases_note: A repeating reference cycle sits within a longer treatment plan. The oncology team chooses the number of cycles and confirms changes; no patient dates are required here.
patient.timeline_note: NCCP defines the treatment days. Symptom bands are broad educational guidance; reactions can occur on any day, and cumulative effects may continue between cycles.
patient.safety_note: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell require immediate contact. Serious symptoms override any timeline or diary.
patient.teachback: Can you explain which visits are planned, whether a pump is involved, and which symptoms mean you should call today? No dates or symptom scores are needed to use this guide.
patient.consent_support: Discuss the treatment aim, alternatives, expected benefit, serious and lasting risks, fertility/pregnancy precautions and the contact plan. Confirm RAS selection for colorectal treatment, infusion premedication, skin care and post-treatment mineral checks. Explain early and delayed diarrhoea separately.
patient.urgent_extra: New breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse, severe diarrhoea or inability to drink require prompt assessment. Report eye pain, blurred vision, blistering or infected skin promptly.

evidence.interpretation: Adding cetuximab to irinotecan improved tumour shrinkage and the time before cancer worsened in a selected trial group. Overall survival was similar between the groups. rationale.summary: EGFR blockade is combined with the topoisomerase-I inhibitor irinotecan to control selected metastatic colorectal cancer.
rationale.setting: Advanced / metastatic colorectal cancer
rationale.line: Second-line RAS-wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer after failure of, or a contraindication to, oxaliplatin-based treatment.
factors: Exact prior therapies and line of treatment
Tumour molecular results and disease distribution
Need for response, fitness, residual toxicity and patient priorities
Ability to attend the schedule and safely manage any infusion pump
alternatives: Discuss other active systemic options, a clinical trial and supportive care in the individual molecular/line-specific setting; this card does not rank all alternatives.
limitations: Retrospective RAS subgroup.
Almost half the irinotecan-only arm subsequently received cetuximab; this complicates overall-survival interpretation but does not establish a hidden survival benefit.
Indirect schedule evidence: EPIC used irinotecan every three weeks; this NCCP regimen uses 180 mg/m² every 14 days. EPIC also used weekly rather than fortnightly cetuximab.

NCCP specifies observations before, during and after initial cetuximab infusions, with one-hour post-infusion observation after the first two doses; subsequent observation follows the regimen, reaction history and current product/local requirements.
First cetuximab infusion must respect the 5 mg/min maximum; subsequent maximum 10 mg/min. Do not promise a fixed two-hour visit for a large fortnightly dose.

evidence.population: Metastatic colorectal cancer after fluoropyrimidine/oxaliplatin; 452 RAS-wild-type patients in a retrospective analysis. Prior irinotecan or EGFR-antibody therapy was excluded.
evidence.comparison: Weekly cetuximab plus irinotecan versus irinotecan alone; irinotecan 350 mg/m² every three weeks, with protocol-specified 300 mg/m² subgroups.
evidence.qualitative_result: Response and progression-free survival improved; overall survival was not significantly different.

evidence.harms: Added EGFR-related skin and infusion toxicity, alongside irinotecan diarrhoea and neutropenia.

patient.title: Fortnightly cetuximab + FOLFIRI

agents.name: Cetuximab
agents.mechanism: Blocks growth messages at the cell surface
agents.explanation: Cetuximab attaches to EGFR on the outside of cells and blocks some growth messages. In this bowel-cancer plan, validated extended RAS testing helps identify whether treatment is suitable. Healthy skin also uses EGFR, so skin and nail effects need early care.
agents.watch: Report rash or sore nails early. Tell the nurse immediately about infusion symptoms. Eye pain, new breathing problems or severe diarrhoea need prompt advice. Blood tests check minerals during treatment and for two months afterwards.
risks: Rash, dry skin, cracks and sore nails
Infusion reaction; rare serious lung or skin effects

agents.name: Irinotecan
agents.explanation: The body converts irinotecan into SN-38. This traps an enzyme called topoisomerase I while DNA is being copied, causing damage that can stop cancer cells dividing. Normal bowel and blood-forming cells can also be affected.
agents.watch: Tell the nurse immediately about cramps, sweating or diarrhoea during the infusion. Diarrhoea starting later needs the separate written treatment and contact plan.
risks: Rare serious lung or allergic reactions

agents.name: Folinic acid
agents.explanation: Folinic acid helps fluorouracil remain bound to an enzyme needed to make DNA. In this regimen it increases fluorouracil activity and can also increase its unwanted effects. It is not a vitamin supplement to start yourself.
agents.watch: The combined treatment can increase mouth soreness and diarrhoea. Report these promptly. Rare allergic reactions can occur.

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil interferes with the production and use of DNA and RNA, the instructions cells need to grow. The infusion extends exposure over approximately two days.
agents.watch: Diarrhoea, mouth sores and skin soreness may become serious. Chest pain during the pump infusion needs emergency assessment. Unexpected severe early toxicity can occur even after DPD testing.
risks: Severe early toxicity including DPD-related toxicity

questions.q: How is my treatment chosen?
questions.a: This combination is used for RAS wild-type bowel cancer that has spread. Your team explains the aim, alternatives and how benefit will be reviewed.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates to understand the cycle?
questions.a: No. The graph explains a general pattern. Your hospital arranges appointments; the guide and its safety information are available without entering anything.

questions.q: Will I have a pump at home?
questions.a: Confirm port/PICC preparation, pump connection, home care and professional disconnection around Day 3.

questions.q: What happens if a dose is delayed?
questions.a: The team checks the cause and may delay, reduce, change or stop one medicine. Ask which component changes and when you should next attend; do not restart yourself.

questions.q: How will I know whether it is helping?
questions.a: Scans, symptoms and clinical review assess benefit. A rash, side effect or good day alone cannot show whether the cancer is responding.

questions.q: What about radiotherapy?
questions.a: This NCCP regimen does not contain a routine radiotherapy course. If radiation is recommended separately, ask whether it is before, during or after these medicines.

questions.q: What about fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding?
questions.a: Discuss fertility preservation and reproductive plans before treatment. Ask for the contraception and breastfeeding instructions for every medicine; the whole regimen may require longer precautions than one medicine alone.

questions.q: Why is RAS testing mentioned?
questions.a: RAS testing selects cetuximab treatment in colorectal cancer. It is not the selection test for the separate head-and-neck radiotherapy indication. Confirm the cancer-specific plan with your team.

patient.phases_note: A repeating reference cycle sits within a longer treatment plan. The oncology team chooses the number of cycles and confirms changes; no patient dates are required here.
patient.timeline_note: NCCP defines the treatment days. Symptom bands are broad educational guidance; reactions can occur on any day, and cumulative effects may continue between cycles.
patient.safety_note: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell require immediate contact. Serious symptoms override any timeline or diary.
patient.teachback: Can you explain which visits are planned, whether a pump is involved, and which symptoms mean you should call today? No dates or symptom scores are needed to use this guide.
patient.consent_support: Discuss the treatment aim, alternatives, expected benefit, serious and lasting risks, fertility/pregnancy precautions and the contact plan. Confirm RAS selection for colorectal treatment, infusion premedication, skin care and post-treatment mineral checks. Explain DPD testing and the exact pump schedule. Explain early and delayed diarrhoea separately.
patient.urgent_extra: New breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse, severe diarrhoea or inability to drink require prompt assessment. Report eye pain, blurred vision, blistering or infected skin promptly. Call for line pain, swelling, leakage or unexpected pump progress.

items.text: Cetuximab on Day 1. Day 1: irinotecan, folinic acid and fluorouracil, then a 46-hour fluorouracil pump; planned disconnection around Day 3. A repeating 14-day cycle. The number of cycles depends on benefit, side effects and your treatment plan.

evidence.title: CRYSTAL: extended RAS analysis
evidence.intro: Studies can help explain why a treatment is offered. The schedule, previous medicines and tumour tests affect how well the evidence fits you.
evidence.population: RAS-wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer; exact line and treatment goal are confirmed by the oncology team.
evidence.interpretation: In a selected bowel-cancer trial, adding cetuximab to FOLFIRI helped more tumours shrink and delayed cancer growth; patients also lived longer as a group. Your cancer biology, previous treatment and health affect the likely benefit. These results cannot predict your own outcome. The main trial used weekly cetuximab, so it is supporting evidence for this fortnightly schedule.

steps.title: Before the first visit
steps.text: Confirm the exact regimen, tests, medicines, emergency number and treatment goal. Discuss which central line is suitable and arrange pump training.

steps.title: At the treatment unit
steps.text: Fortnightly cetuximab infusion time is set from the dose and safe infusion rate; the first dose may take longer. Irinotecan usually takes about 90 minutes. Blood review, preparation, premedicines and observation add time; infusion time is not the total appointment length.

steps.title: After the infusion
steps.text: The fluorouracil pump runs for about 46 hours. Confirm where and when it will be disconnected, usually around Day 3; do not disconnect it yourself unless specifically trained.

steps.title: Between doses
steps.text: Use the written symptom and support plan; do not wait for the next appointment if urgent symptoms appear.

steps.title: The next decision
steps.text: Confirm the next visit after any delay or dose change. Treatment continues only while the oncology team judges benefit and tolerability acceptable. Follow-up mineral checks continue after the final EGFR-antibody dose where applicable.

milestones.clinical: Confirm diagnosis, treatment line, goal, prior treatments, performance status, consent and all medicines. Baseline FBC, renal and liver profile; assess infection, hydration, bowel symptoms and previous treatment toxicity. Document validated extended RAS wild-type status for this colorectal pathway; do not infer it from unknown or KRAS exon 2-only testing. Measure electrolytes including magnesium, calcium and potassium before treatment; correct abnormalities according to the prescription. Ask specifically about prior antibody infusion reactions, red-meat allergy, tick bites and any known cetuximab IgE findings. Document DPD assessment before the first fluorouracil dose unless already tested. Complete DPD deficiency excludes fluorouracil; partial deficiency needs a specialist dose plan. ECG if cardiac function is compromised; no universal serial echo schedule is imposed. Confirm safe central access and pump training. In moderate/severe renal impairment, elevated uracil can misclassify DPD phenotype; consider genotype testing as directed in the current NCCP source. Review prior severe diarrhoea, bowel disease/obstruction, bilirubin and known UGT1A1*28 status. A genotype-related starting-dose decision is individualized.

patient.title: Weekly cetuximab + FOLFOX-4

agents.name: Cetuximab
agents.mechanism: Blocks growth messages at the cell surface
agents.explanation: Cetuximab attaches to EGFR on the outside of cells and blocks some growth messages. In this bowel-cancer plan, validated extended RAS testing helps identify whether treatment is suitable. Healthy skin also uses EGFR, so skin and nail effects need early care.
agents.watch: Report rash or sore nails early. Tell the nurse immediately about infusion symptoms. Eye pain, new breathing problems or severe diarrhoea need prompt advice. Blood tests check minerals during treatment and for two months afterwards.
risks: Rash, dry skin, cracks and sore nails
Infusion reaction; rare serious lung or skin effects

agents.name: Oxaliplatin
agents.explanation: Oxaliplatin makes links within DNA. These interfere with copying and repair, which can stop a cancer cell dividing. Healthy tissues can also be affected.
agents.watch: Cold can trigger tingling or throat discomfort. Tell the team about persistent numbness, difficulty with buttons or walking, or infusion symptoms. New breathing difficulty always needs assessment.
risks: Persistent sensory neuropathy, sometimes lasting after treatment
Rare serious lung or blood complications

agents.name: Folinic acid
agents.explanation: Folinic acid helps fluorouracil remain bound to an enzyme needed to make DNA. In this regimen it increases fluorouracil activity and can also increase its unwanted effects. It is not a vitamin supplement to start yourself.
agents.watch: The combined treatment can increase mouth soreness and diarrhoea. Report these promptly. Rare allergic reactions can occur.

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil interferes with the production and use of DNA and RNA, the instructions cells need to grow. The infusion extends exposure over approximately two days.
agents.watch: Diarrhoea, mouth sores and skin soreness may become serious. Chest pain during the pump infusion needs emergency assessment. Unexpected severe early toxicity can occur even after DPD testing.
risks: Severe early toxicity including DPD-related toxicity

questions.q: How is my treatment chosen?
questions.a: This combination is used for RAS wild-type bowel cancer that has spread. Your team explains the aim, alternatives and how benefit will be reviewed.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates to understand the cycle?
questions.a: No. The graph explains a general pattern. Your hospital arranges appointments; the guide and its safety information are available without entering anything.

questions.q: Will I have a pump at home?
questions.a: Arrange Day 2 infusion renewal and final disconnection around Day 3. This is two separate 22-hour infusions; do not use a 46-hour pump timetable.

questions.q: What happens if a dose is delayed?
questions.a: The team checks the cause and may delay, reduce, change or stop one medicine. Ask which component changes and when you should next attend; do not restart yourself.

questions.q: How will I know whether it is helping?
questions.a: Scans, symptoms and clinical review assess benefit. A rash, side effect or good day alone cannot show whether the cancer is responding.

questions.q: What about radiotherapy?
questions.a: This NCCP regimen does not contain a routine radiotherapy course. If radiation is recommended separately, ask whether it is before, during or after these medicines.

questions.q: What about fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding?
questions.a: Discuss fertility preservation and reproductive plans before treatment. Ask for the contraception and breastfeeding instructions for every medicine; the whole regimen may require longer precautions than one medicine alone.

questions.q: Why is RAS testing mentioned?
questions.a: RAS testing selects cetuximab treatment in colorectal cancer. It is not the selection test for the separate head-and-neck radiotherapy indication. Confirm the cancer-specific plan with your team.

questions.q: Why is Day 2 different from other FOLFOX leaflets?
questions.a: NCCP FOLFOX-4 has fluorouracil on Days 1 and 2, each with a 22-hour infusion. It is not modified FOLFOX-6. The team confirms your Day 2 prescription and visit; do not rely on another FOLFOX schedule.

patient.phases_note: A repeating reference cycle sits within a longer treatment plan. The oncology team chooses the number of cycles and confirms changes; no patient dates are required here.
patient.timeline_note: NCCP defines the treatment days. Symptom bands are broad educational guidance; reactions can occur on any day, and cumulative effects may continue between cycles.
patient.safety_note: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell require immediate contact. Serious symptoms override any timeline or diary.
patient.teachback: Can you explain which visits are planned, whether a pump is involved, and which symptoms mean you should call today? No dates or symptom scores are needed to use this guide.
patient.consent_support: Discuss the treatment aim, alternatives, expected benefit, serious and lasting risks, fertility/pregnancy precautions and the contact plan. Confirm RAS selection for colorectal treatment, infusion premedication, skin care and post-treatment mineral checks. Explain DPD testing and the exact pump schedule.
patient.urgent_extra: New breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse, severe diarrhoea or inability to drink require prompt assessment. Report eye pain, blurred vision, blistering or infected skin promptly. Call for line pain, swelling, leakage or unexpected pump progress.

items.text: Cetuximab on Day 1 and Day 8. Day 1: oxaliplatin and folinic acid, then fluorouracil bolus and a 22-hour infusion. steps.title: Before the first visit
steps.text: Confirm the exact regimen, tests, medicines, emergency number and treatment goal. Discuss which central line is suitable and arrange pump training.

steps.title: At the treatment unit
steps.text: The first weekly cetuximab infusion takes about two hours; later weekly infusions usually take about one hour. Oxaliplatin and folinic acid are usually infused over about two hours, before fluorouracil. Blood review, preparation, premedicines and observation add time; infusion time is not the total appointment length.

steps.title: After the infusion
steps.text: Return on Day 2 for the second folinic-acid/fluorouracil part and renewal of the second 22-hour infusion. Final disconnection is planned around Day 3. This FOLFOX4 plan is not a single 46-hour infusion.

steps.title: Between doses
steps.text: Attend the separate Day 8 cetuximab-only visit. This is not another irinotecan or oxaliplatin day. Use the written symptom and support plan; do not wait for the next appointment if urgent symptoms appear.

steps.title: The next decision
steps.text: Confirm the next visit after any delay or dose change. Treatment continues only while the oncology team judges benefit and tolerability acceptable. Follow-up mineral checks continue after the final EGFR-antibody dose where applicable.

details.title: Transport and daily life
details.text: Plan transport if antihistamines, symptoms or other medicines affect driving. Ask for practical, work, nutrition or emotional support.

details.title: If treatment changes
details.text: Ask which component has been held and which visits remain. A treatment delay does not automatically cancel blood tests, line care or symptom follow-up.

patient.title: Cetuximab · every two weeks

agents.name: Cetuximab
agents.mechanism: Blocks growth messages at the cell surface
agents.explanation: Cetuximab attaches to EGFR on the outside of cells and blocks some growth messages. In this bowel-cancer plan, validated extended RAS testing helps identify whether treatment is suitable. Healthy skin also uses EGFR, so skin and nail effects need early care.
agents.watch: Report rash or sore nails early. Tell the nurse immediately about infusion symptoms. Eye pain, new breathing problems or severe diarrhoea need prompt advice. Blood tests check minerals during treatment and for two months afterwards.
risks: Rash, dry skin, cracks and sore nails
Infusion reaction; rare serious lung or skin effects

questions.q: How is my treatment chosen?
questions.a: Cetuximab alone is an option for RAS wild-type bowel cancer that has spread after oxaliplatin and irinotecan have failed, when irinotecan cannot be tolerated. Your team explains the aim, alternatives and how benefit will be reviewed.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates to understand the cycle?
questions.a: No. The graph explains a general pattern. Your hospital arranges appointments; the guide and its safety information are available without entering anything.

questions.q: Will I have a pump at home?
questions.a: There is no home fluorouracil pump in this regimen. Your team chooses a cannula or central line based on your veins and wider treatment plan.

questions.q: What happens if a dose is delayed?
questions.a: The team checks the cause and may delay, reduce, change or stop one medicine. Ask which component changes and when you should next attend; do not restart yourself.

questions.q: How will I know whether it is helping?
questions.a: Scans, symptoms and clinical review assess benefit. A rash, side effect or good day alone cannot show whether the cancer is responding.

questions.q: What about radiotherapy?
questions.a: This NCCP regimen does not contain a routine radiotherapy course. If radiation is recommended separately, ask whether it is before, during or after these medicines.

questions.q: What about fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding?
questions.a: Discuss fertility preservation and reproductive plans before treatment. Ask for the contraception and breastfeeding instructions for every medicine; the whole regimen may require longer precautions than one medicine alone.

questions.q: Why is RAS testing mentioned?
questions.a: RAS testing selects cetuximab treatment in colorectal cancer. It is not the selection test for the separate head-and-neck radiotherapy indication. Confirm the cancer-specific plan with your team.

patient.phases_note: A repeating reference cycle sits within a longer treatment plan. The oncology team chooses the number of cycles and confirms changes; no patient dates are required here.
patient.timeline_note: NCCP defines the treatment days. Symptom bands are broad educational guidance; reactions can occur on any day, and cumulative effects may continue between cycles.
patient.safety_note: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell require immediate contact. Serious symptoms override any timeline or diary.
patient.teachback: Can you explain which visits are planned, whether a pump is involved, and which symptoms mean you should call today? No dates or symptom scores are needed to use this guide.
patient.consent_support: Discuss the treatment aim, alternatives, expected benefit, serious and lasting risks, fertility/pregnancy precautions and the contact plan. Confirm RAS selection for colorectal treatment, infusion premedication, skin care and post-treatment mineral checks.
patient.urgent_extra: New breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse, severe diarrhoea or inability to drink require prompt assessment. Report eye pain, blurred vision, blistering or infected skin promptly.

agents.name: Cetuximab
agents.mechanism: Blocks growth messages at the cell surface
agents.explanation: Cetuximab attaches to EGFR on the outside of cells and blocks some growth messages. In this bowel-cancer plan, validated extended RAS testing helps identify whether treatment is suitable. Healthy skin also uses EGFR, so skin and nail effects need early care.
agents.watch: Report rash or sore nails early. Tell the nurse immediately about infusion symptoms. Eye pain, new breathing problems or severe diarrhoea need prompt advice. Blood tests check minerals during treatment and for two months afterwards.
risks: Rash, dry skin, cracks and sore nails
Infusion reaction; rare serious lung or skin effects

agents.name: Oxaliplatin
agents.explanation: Oxaliplatin makes links within DNA. These interfere with copying and repair, which can stop a cancer cell dividing. Healthy tissues can also be affected.
agents.watch: Cold can trigger tingling or throat discomfort. Tell the team about persistent numbness, difficulty with buttons or walking, or infusion symptoms. New breathing difficulty always needs assessment.
risks: Persistent sensory neuropathy, sometimes lasting after treatment
Rare serious lung or blood complications

agents.name: Folinic acid
agents.explanation: Folinic acid helps fluorouracil remain bound to an enzyme needed to make DNA. In this regimen it increases fluorouracil activity and can also increase its unwanted effects. It is not a vitamin supplement to start yourself.
agents.watch: The combined treatment can increase mouth soreness and diarrhoea. Report these promptly. Rare allergic reactions can occur.

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil interferes with the production and use of DNA and RNA, the instructions cells need to grow. The infusion extends exposure over approximately two days.
agents.watch: Diarrhoea, mouth sores and skin soreness may become serious. Chest pain during the pump infusion needs emergency assessment. Unexpected severe early toxicity can occur even after DPD testing.
risks: Severe early toxicity including DPD-related toxicity

questions.q: How is my treatment chosen?
questions.a: This combination is used for RAS wild-type bowel cancer that has spread. Your team explains the aim, alternatives and how benefit will be reviewed.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates to understand the cycle?
questions.a: No. The graph explains a general pattern. Your hospital arranges appointments; the guide and its safety information are available without entering anything.

questions.q: Will I have a pump at home?
questions.a: Confirm port/PICC preparation, pump connection, home care and professional disconnection around Day 3.

questions.q: What happens if a dose is delayed?
questions.a: The team checks the cause and may delay, reduce, change or stop one medicine. Ask which component changes and when you should next attend; do not restart yourself.

questions.q: How will I know whether it is helping?
questions.a: Scans, symptoms and clinical review assess benefit. A rash, side effect or good day alone cannot show whether the cancer is responding.

questions.q: What about radiotherapy?
questions.a: This NCCP regimen does not contain a routine radiotherapy course. If radiation is recommended separately, ask whether it is before, during or after these medicines.

questions.q: What about fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding?
questions.a: Discuss fertility preservation and reproductive plans before treatment. Ask for the contraception and breastfeeding instructions for every medicine; the whole regimen may require longer precautions than one medicine alone.

questions.q: Why is RAS testing mentioned?
questions.a: RAS testing selects cetuximab treatment in colorectal cancer. It is not the selection test for the separate head-and-neck radiotherapy indication. Confirm the cancer-specific plan with your team.

patient.phases_note: A repeating reference cycle sits within a longer treatment plan. The oncology team chooses the number of cycles and confirms changes; no patient dates are required here.
patient.timeline_note: NCCP defines the treatment days. Symptom bands are broad educational guidance; reactions can occur on any day, and cumulative effects may continue between cycles.
patient.safety_note: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell require immediate contact. Serious symptoms override any timeline or diary.
patient.teachback: Can you explain which visits are planned, whether a pump is involved, and which symptoms mean you should call today? No dates or symptom scores are needed to use this guide.

Confirm RAS selection for colorectal treatment, infusion premedication, skin care and post-treatment mineral checks. Explain DPD testing and the exact pump schedule.
patient.urgent_extra: New breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse, severe diarrhoea or inability to drink require prompt assessment. Report eye pain, blurred vision, blistering or infected skin promptly. Call for line pain, swelling, leakage or unexpected pump progress.

evidence.title: OPUS: exploratory extended RAS analysis
evidence.intro: Studies can help explain why a treatment is offered. The schedule, previous medicines and tumour tests affect how well the evidence fits you.
evidence.population: Metastatic colorectal cancer with validated extended RAS-wild-type status. The NCCP document retains older KRAS wording; the current Erbitux SmPC requires extended RAS testing.
evidence.interpretation: Adding cetuximab to FOLFOX4 improved tumour shrinkage in a small selected trial group. That analysis did not establish a clear survival advantage. Tumour shrinkage is not the same as cure. The trial used weekly cetuximab and FOLFOX4, so its results are indirect for this fortnightly modified FOLFOX6 plan.

steps.text: Fortnightly cetuximab infusion time is set from the dose and safe infusion rate; the first dose may take longer. rationale.summary: EGFR blockade is combined with the oxaliplatin/fluorouracil/folinic-acid FOLFOX backbone to control selected metastatic colorectal cancer.
rationale.setting: Advanced / metastatic colorectal cancer
rationale.line: Metastatic colorectal cancer with validated extended RAS-wild-type status. The NCCP document retains older KRAS wording; the current Erbitux SmPC requires extended RAS testing.
factors: Exact prior therapies and line of treatment
Tumour molecular results and disease distribution
Need for response, fitness, residual toxicity and patient priorities
Ability to attend the schedule and safely manage any infusion pump
alternatives: Discuss other active systemic options, a clinical trial and supportive care in the individual molecular/line-specific setting; this card does not rank all alternatives.
limitations: Small retrospective subgroup; 38 combination and 49 chemotherapy-only patients.
Do not treat a response endpoint as cure or as an overall-survival gain.
Indirect for both schedule and backbone: OPUS used weekly cetuximab with FOLFOX4, not fortnightly cetuximab with modified FOLFOX6. Do not relabel OPUS results as an exact 00733 trial.

evidence.population: First-line metastatic colorectal cancer; 87 extended RAS-wild-type patients in a randomized phase II trial subgroup.
evidence.comparison: Weekly cetuximab plus FOLFOX4 versus FOLFOX4.
evidence.qualitative_result: Tumour response improved. The small extended-RAS subgroup did not establish statistically significant progression-free or overall-survival benefit.
limitations: Small retrospective subgroup; 38 combination and 49 chemotherapy-only patients.
Do not treat a response endpoint as cure or as an overall-survival gain.
evidence.harms: Cetuximab adds EGFR-related toxicity; the chemotherapy backbone adds myelosuppression, mucositis and cumulative oxaliplatin neuropathy.

patient.title: Panitumumab

agents.name: Panitumumab
agents.mechanism: Blocks growth messages at the cell surface
agents.explanation: Panitumumab attaches to EGFR, a receptor on the outside of cells. This can interrupt signals that help some bowel cancers grow. A tumour RAS test helps identify whether this approach is suitable. EGFR also supports healthy skin, which explains why skin and nail changes need attention.
agents.watch: Report rash, painful cracks or nail changes early. Eye pain or blurred vision, new breathing symptoms, severe diarrhoea, or blistering skin need prompt assessment. Blood tests check minerals such as magnesium.
risks: Rash, dry skin, cracks and sore nails
Infusion reaction; rare serious lung or skin effects

questions.q: Why do I need a RAS test?
questions.a: RAS is part of the growth-signalling pathway inside cancer cells. If it is changed by a mutation, blocking EGFR is unlikely to help. Your team needs a validated wild-type RAS result before panitumumab. Other tumour tests and the treatment aim also affect the choice.

questions.q: Is this the same as checkpoint immunotherapy?
questions.a: Panitumumab is a targeted antibody against EGFR. It works differently from checkpoint treatments used in some other cancer regimens. Ask your team which treatment class and side effects apply to you.

questions.q: Does a rash mean the treatment is working?
questions.a: A rash is a recognised drug effect, but it cannot tell you whether your cancer is responding. Report it early so it can be treated. Scans, symptoms and clinical review guide the response assessment.

questions.q: Will I need radiotherapy as part of this cycle?
questions.a: These panitumumab regimens do not contain a scheduled radiotherapy course. If radiotherapy is recommended separately, your oncology teams will explain its purpose and timing. Do not assume it occurs on infusion or pump days.

questions.q: What about pregnancy, breastfeeding or fertility?
questions.a: Discuss pregnancy plans and fertility before treatment. Panitumumab requires contraception during treatment and for two months afterwards, and breastfeeding should be avoided for that period. When chemotherapy is also included, its precautions may last longer; ask for the instructions for the whole regimen.

questions.q: How long should I allow for the appointment?
questions.a: The infusion itself is usually about an hour at first, but blood tests, review, pharmacy preparation and observation add time. Ask your unit for its expected visit length. Larger doses or a previous reaction may need a longer infusion.

chapters.title: Your treatment aim and review plan
chapters.intro: Understand why this option fits your cancer.

items.title: The setting matters
items.text: Panitumumab is used for bowel cancer that has spread and has a confirmed wild-type RAS result. It is given after earlier fluoropyrimidine, oxaliplatin and irinotecan treatment has failed. Your team explains the aim, alternatives and how benefit will be reviewed.

items.title: What the tumour tests mean
items.text: RAS wild type is required for panitumumab. Your team also considers the cancer location, other molecular results, previous treatment and whether surgery or other local treatment could be useful. A positive eligibility result is not a promise of benefit.

chapters.title: Before you start and before each cycle
chapters.intro: The team checks that the plan remains suitable.

items.title: Checks and medicines
items.text: Review blood counts, kidney/liver function and minerals, current symptoms, allergies and all medicines. DPD testing is not a requirement for panitumumab alone.

items.title: Skin, eyes and breathing
items.text: Tell the team about an existing rash, skin infection, dry or painful eyes, contact lenses, or previous lung inflammation. Report new eye pain, light sensitivity or visual change promptly.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: Build the plan around what matters to you.

items.title: Skin and nails
items.text: Ask for your skin-care plan before the first infusion. Use the recommended moisturiser and sun protection; your team may prescribe a cream or an antibiotic. Do not use ordinary acne treatments without advice. Avoid friction on sore skin and tell the team about painful nail folds.

items.title: Food, activity and support
items.text: Keep fluids and nourishing food within reach. Pace activity around energy levels and ask for dietetic, emotional or practical support. If symptoms prevent eating, drinking or usual tasks, contact the team.

items.title: Pregnancy and fertility
items.text: Discuss pregnancy plans and fertility before treatment. Panitumumab requires contraception during treatment and for two months afterwards, and breastfeeding should be avoided for that period. When chemotherapy is also included, its precautions may last longer; ask for the instructions for the whole regimen.

chapters.title: When treatment changes or finishes
chapters.intro: Follow-up continues after the last infusion.

items.title: Monitoring and recovery
items.text: Continue your skin plan and planned magnesium, calcium and potassium checks for about eight weeks after panitumumab. New symptoms still need review. Ask when to stop prescribed supportive medicines.

items.title: Treatment choices
items.text: Your team may pause, reduce, change or stop one or more medicines. Ask which medicine changes, why, and what the next review will assess. Supportive and palliative care can help alongside active treatment.

chapters.title: Recognise changes early
chapters.intro: You do not need to identify the responsible medicine before asking for help.

items.title: When to call
items.text: Report new breathing difficulty, eye pain or blurred vision, blistering or infected skin, severe diarrhoea or dehydration promptly.

items.title: Track impact, not just a score
items.text: Describe when symptoms began, whether they are worsening, and whether they affect food, fluids, sleep, walking or daily tasks. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Use the passport if it helps; it is not required to access this information.

chapters.title: Visits, access and coordination
chapters.intro: Know what happens in the clinic and what happens at home.

support.title: Start skin care early

support.title: Minerals and blood tests
support.text: Panitumumab can lower magnesium and other minerals even when you feel well. Blood tests continue during treatment and for about eight weeks after it finishes. Take replacement treatment only as prescribed.

support.title: Feeling sick or loose stools
support.text: Panitumumab has low nausea risk, but symptoms can still occur. Follow the rescue medicine and hydration plan from your team. Severe or persistent diarrhoea, reduced urine or inability to drink needs urgent advice.

support.title: Travel and daily life
support.text: Allow time for blood tests, review, preparation, infusion and observation. Ask about transport if medicines or symptoms affect driving. Pace activity and seek help with food, work or caring responsibilities.

support.title: The whole treatment plan
support.text: Ask how and when the team will assess benefit, which blood tests continue during a pause, and what happens after the final dose. Mineral checks continue monthly for two months after the last antibody treatment.

evidence.title: 20100007: panitumumab monotherapy
evidence.intro: Studies can help explain why a treatment is offered. The schedule, previous medicines and tumour tests affect how well the evidence fits you.
evidence.population: Adult RAS-wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer as monotherapy after failure of fluoropyrimidine-, oxaliplatin- and irinotecan-containing chemotherapy.
evidence.interpretation: Panitumumab improved survival in a trial group selected using tumour testing after other bowel-cancer medicines had stopped working. The likely benefit for you depends on your cancer, previous treatment and general health; it cannot be predicted from the trial alone.

agents.name: Irinotecan
agents.explanation: The body converts irinotecan into SN-38. This traps an enzyme called topoisomerase I while DNA is being copied, causing damage that can stop cancer cells dividing. Normal bowel and blood-forming cells can also be affected.
agents.watch: Tell the nurse immediately about cramps, sweating or diarrhoea during the infusion. Diarrhoea starting later needs the separate written treatment and contact plan.
risks: Rare serious lung or allergic reactions

questions.q: How is my treatment chosen?
questions.a: Irinotecan alone is used for advanced bowel cancer after a fluorouracil-containing treatment has failed. Your team explains the aim, alternatives and how benefit will be reviewed.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates to understand the cycle?
questions.a: No. The graph explains a general pattern. Your hospital arranges appointments; the guide and its safety information are available without entering anything.

questions.q: Will I have a pump at home?
questions.a: There is no home fluorouracil pump in this regimen. Your team chooses a cannula or central line based on your veins and wider treatment plan.

questions.q: What happens if a dose is delayed?
questions.a: The team checks the cause and may delay, reduce, change or stop one medicine. Ask which component changes and when you should next attend; do not restart yourself.

questions.q: How will I know whether it is helping?
questions.a: Scans, symptoms and clinical review assess benefit. A rash, side effect or good day alone cannot show whether the cancer is responding.

questions.q: What about radiotherapy?
questions.a: This NCCP regimen does not contain a routine radiotherapy course. If radiation is recommended separately, ask whether it is before, during or after these medicines.

questions.q: What about fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding?
questions.a: Discuss fertility preservation and reproductive plans before treatment. Ask for the contraception and breastfeeding instructions for every medicine; the whole regimen may require longer precautions than one medicine alone.

patient.phases_note: A repeating reference cycle sits within a longer treatment plan. The oncology team chooses the number of cycles and confirms changes; no patient dates are required here.
patient.timeline_note: NCCP defines the treatment days. Symptom bands are broad educational guidance; reactions can occur on any day, and cumulative effects may continue between cycles.
patient.safety_note: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell require immediate contact. Serious symptoms override any timeline or diary.
patient.teachback: Can you explain which visits are planned, whether a pump is involved, and which symptoms mean you should call today? No dates or symptom scores are needed to use this guide.
patient.consent_support: Discuss the treatment aim, alternatives, expected benefit, serious and lasting risks, fertility/pregnancy precautions and the contact plan. Explain early and delayed diarrhoea separately.
patient.urgent_extra: New breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse, severe diarrhoea or inability to drink require prompt assessment.

agents.name: Oxaliplatin
agents.explanation: Oxaliplatin makes links within DNA. These interfere with copying and repair, which can stop a cancer cell dividing. Healthy tissues can also be affected.
agents.watch: Cold can trigger tingling or throat discomfort. Tell the team about persistent numbness, difficulty with buttons or walking, or infusion symptoms. New breathing difficulty always needs assessment.
risks: Persistent sensory neuropathy, sometimes lasting after treatment
Rare serious lung or blood complications

agents.name: Folinic acid
agents.explanation: Folinic acid helps fluorouracil remain bound to an enzyme needed to make DNA. In this regimen it increases fluorouracil activity and can also increase its unwanted effects. It is not a vitamin supplement to start yourself.
agents.watch: The combined treatment can increase mouth soreness and diarrhoea. Report these promptly. Rare allergic reactions can occur.

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil interferes with the production and use of DNA and RNA, the instructions cells need to grow. The infusion extends exposure over approximately two days.
agents.watch: Diarrhoea, mouth sores and skin soreness may become serious. Chest pain during the pump infusion needs emergency assessment. Unexpected severe early toxicity can occur even after DPD testing.
risks: Severe early toxicity including DPD-related toxicity

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

patient.phases_note: The treating team confirms the indication, schedule and duration. Changes are recorded on your own prescription.

patient.safety_note: There are no guaranteed safe days. Act on fever, sudden illness or a new serious symptom whenever it occurs. Do not wait for the next appointment.
patient.teachback: Can you explain which medicines you are receiving, the schedule, the contact plan and the symptoms that need prompt help?
patient.consent_support: Confirm DPD testing, pump and line care, disconnection arrangements, cold precautions and anti-sickness instructions.
patient.urgent_extra: New chest pain, breathing difficulty, severe diarrhoea, inability to drink, reduced urine, uncontrolled bleeding or a rapidly worsening symptom needs prompt assessment.

items.title: After colon-cancer surgery
items.text: Adjuvant treatment aims to reduce recurrence risk after complete resection. The likely absolute benefit depends on stage, pathology, fitness and other features. Ask how recurrence risk and neuropathy risk influence the proposed duration.

items.title: Advanced colorectal or upper-GI cancer
items.text: Treatment may aim to control growth, relieve symptoms and prolong life. The plan is reviewed against response, toxicity and your priorities. A treatment break or a change of components requires an individual discussion.

items.title: How long will treatment last?
items.text: Do not infer duration from the number of passport pages. Ask for the planned number of cycles and review points. The NCCP schedule distinguishes adjuvant colon treatment, metastatic colorectal treatment and upper-GI treatment.

chapters.title: Living with the 46-hour pump
chapters.intro: Ask for a demonstration and written contact instructions.

items.title: Before leaving
items.text: Know what normal pump progress looks like, how to carry it and how to protect the line while washing or sleeping. Check who will disconnect it and when. Have the team check anything you do not understand.

items.title: Leakage or a delivery problem
items.text: Use the hospital spill instructions, avoid direct contact with leaked medicine and call the team. Do not repair a connection or adjust the pump. A pump finishing much sooner or later than expected also needs advice.

items.title: Chest pain while on fluorouracil
items.text: Fluorouracil can affect the heart. New chest pain during treatment needs urgent assessment; severe pain, collapse or major breathing difficulty means 112/999. Tell emergency staff that fluorouracil is infusing. Follow the team’s instructions about the pump.

chapters.intro: Symptoms, blood results and the treatment aim answer different questions.

items.title: Blood counts
items.text: Neutrophils protect against infection, haemoglobin carries oxygen and platelets help clotting. A normal previous result or feeling well does not prove the current counts are safe. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate advice.

items.title: Kidney and liver function
items.text: Organ function can change drug exposure. Vomiting or diarrhoea can cause dehydration and worsen kidney function. Report reduced urine, poor intake, jaundice and new medicines. The clinical assessment combines results with symptoms.

items.title: Describe symptoms in practical terms
items.text: Tell the team about the worst symptoms since the last visit, even if improved today. Examples include extra stools above your usual pattern, whether mouth pain affects drinking, and whether numbness affects buttons or balance.

items.title: How benefit is assessed
items.text: After surgery, treatment aims to reduce the chance of recurrence; there may be no visible cancer to measure. In advanced disease, scans, symptoms and function help assess control. Ask when review is planned and what would lead to a change.

chapters.title: Recognising treatment effects
chapters.intro: Early reporting helps the team manage symptoms and protect function.

items.title: Acute cold sensitivity and persistent neuropathy
items.text: Cold-related tingling can occur soon after oxaliplatin. Persistent numbness between cycles is different and may worsen with repeated treatment. Describe duration and effect on hand use or walking. Some neuropathy can remain after treatment ends.

items.title: Bowel and mouth symptoms
items.text: Fluorouracil can affect rapidly renewing tissues. Keep track of stools compared with your normal pattern, including stoma output. Report diarrhoea, painful ulcers or reduced drinking; do not wait for the next cycle if you are dehydrated or unwell.

items.title: Hand-foot soreness and skin changes
items.text: Tell the team about red, tender or peeling palms or soles. Reduce friction and use the skin care recommended locally. Pain limiting normal activity needs review. Do not assume it must be tolerated to complete treatment.

items.title: Fatigue and nausea
items.text: Use manageable activity, rest and the prescribed anti-sickness plan. New profound weakness, faintness or breathlessness warrants assessment because anaemia, infection, dehydration and other problems can look like ordinary fatigue.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: Plan around the activities and people that matter to you.

items.title: Food, drink and practical help
items.text: Use foods and drinks you can manage. Tell the team about weight loss, poor intake or difficulty shopping and cooking; ask for dietitian or practical support. A fixed daily fluid target is not appropriate for everyone, particularly with heart or kidney problems.

items.title: Activity, rest and driving
items.text: Balance rest with manageable activity. Record what fatigue stops you doing. Do not drive when dizzy, unwell or affected by sedating medicines. Ask about work adjustments and transport for treatment days.

items.title: Medicines, vaccines and supplements
items.text: Bring a complete medicine list, including over-the-counter products and supplements. Ask the oncology pharmacist before changes. Discuss vaccination timing. Do not stop prescribed long-term medicines on your own.

items.title: Fertility, contraception and breastfeeding
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment when relevant. Ask for a written contraception and breastfeeding plan covering each medicine and the period after treatment. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy.

items.title: Support for you and your family
items.text: Ask about psycho-oncology, social work, counselling and symptom support. Take information in manageable amounts. A family member or trusted person can help record questions if you wish. Discuss how treatment fits your priorities.

chapters.title: Words you may hear
chapters.intro: A short reference for clinic discussions.

items.title: Adjuvant, metastatic and cycle
items.text: Adjuvant means treatment after the main treatment, usually surgery, to reduce recurrence risk. Metastatic means spread to a distant site. A cycle includes treatment and the interval before the next planned start.

items.title: DPD, neuropathy and dose modification
items.text: DPD is an enzyme involved in fluorouracil breakdown. Neuropathy means nerve damage or dysfunction. Dose modification means changing the amount, timing or components to balance benefit and harm.

patient.purpose: Modified FOLFOX-6 combines oxaliplatin, folinic acid and fluorouracil. It can be used after colon-cancer surgery or to treat advanced colorectal, stomach or gastro-oesophageal-junction cancer. The aim and duration depend on the indication; ask which applies to you.

day_groups.title: Infusion and pump connection
day_groups.body: Symptoms and blood tests are reviewed. The day-ward medicines are followed by connection of a fluorouracil pump. Tell the nurse immediately about a reaction or pain at the infusion site.
day_groups.action: Before leaving, confirm the pump-care instructions, disconnection appointment and contact number.

day_groups.title: The pump is delivering treatment
day_groups.body: The infusion runs for about 46 hours from connection; the calendar day does not determine the exact finish time. Follow the instructions for keeping the line dry and secure. Avoid cold exposure if it triggers symptoms.
day_groups.action: Call for a leaking, disconnected or unexpectedly stopped pump. Do not reconnect, alter settings or disconnect it yourself unless specifically trained and instructed.

day_groups.title: After disconnection
day_groups.body: Nausea, diarrhoea, mouth symptoms, fatigue or cold sensitivity may continue. Use prescribed support. New symptoms deserve advice even if the pump has finished.
day_groups.action: Report poor intake, persistent diarrhoea or mouth pain early. Chest pain or major breathing difficulty requires emergency help.

day_groups.title: Between visits and the next review
day_groups.body: Blood counts can fall between visits. Numbness may accumulate over cycles. Describe any difficulty fastening buttons, walking or handling objects before more oxaliplatin.
day_groups.action: Bring the symptom passport and check the next appointment. Day 1 usually repeats 14 days after this cycle started, only if confirmed.

support.title: Nausea prevention and rescue
support.text: Take the prescribed prevention medicines at the planned times and keep rescue treatment available. Tell the team if nausea or constipation is not controlled; do not duplicate steroid or anti-sickness medicines.

support.title: Bowel symptoms
support.text: Report diarrhoea promptly and follow the written rescue plan. Severe symptoms, fever, dehydration or inability to drink need urgent advice.

support.title: Counts and recovery
support.text: White-cell growth-factor injections are prescribed according to individual risk and previous complications. They are not automatically required for every patient or every cycle.

support.title: Cold and nerve symptoms
support.text: Avoid cold exposure as advised after oxaliplatin. Report persistent numbness or difficulty with buttons, walking or everyday tasks before the next dose.

evidence.title: Understanding the evidence
evidence.intro: Ask which evidence matches your cancer, treatment aim and medicines.
evidence.interpretation: Adding oxaliplatin to fluorouracil-based treatment improved long-term outcomes in a study of people with stage III colon cancer after surgery. That study used FOLFOX4, a related but different schedule. It does not predict benefit for every indication of modified FOLFOX6 or for an individual person.

chronology_notes.title: Treatment and pump
chronology_notes.text: Day 1 treatment is followed by a 46-hour fluorouracil infusion. The team confirms the exact pump disconnection time.

chronology_notes.title: Cold sensitivity
chronology_notes.text: Tingling or throat discomfort can occur early and may persist; follow the precautions your team gives you.

chronology_notes.title: Blood counts
chronology_notes.text: Counts can fall between visits. The day of the cycle and how well you feel cannot rule out infection.

chronology_notes.title: Symptoms over time
chronology_notes.text: Mouth and bowel symptoms or fatigue can overlap. Numbness may accumulate across cycles; describe changes before the next dose.

patient.administration_text: Oxaliplatin and folinic acid are administered intravenously on day 1. Fluorouracil includes an intravenous bolus and a continuous 46-hour infusion.

sections.title: Before the first treatment
sections.text: Confirm the aim, likely course length, blood-test arrangements and a working urgent contact number. DPD testing is required before starting the fluoropyrimidine unless already completed.

sections.title: Line and pump arrangements
sections.text: Confirm venous access, the 46-hour fluorouracil pump and disconnection arrangements before leaving. Know whom to contact for leakage, an alarm, line pain or a pump that finishes unexpectedly.

sections.title: If treatment is delayed
sections.text: Ask the unit to confirm the new treatment and blood-test dates. Re-anchor supportive medicines to the treatment actually given; do not take an extra or catch-up anticancer dose yourself.

sections.title: Getting help between visits
sections.text: Follow your oncology unit’s urgent advice for fever, infection, severe diarrhoea, chest pain or difficulty breathing. Bring your treatment card and current medicines list.

clinical.component_rationale: Oxaliplatin produces platinum–DNA cross-links. Fluorouracil disrupts thymidylate synthesis and nucleic-acid function, while folinic acid stabilises the fluorouracil–thymidylate-synthase complex and increases fluorouracil activity.

patient.title: FOLFOX-4

agents.name: Oxaliplatin
agents.explanation: Oxaliplatin makes links within DNA. These interfere with copying and repair, which can stop a cancer cell dividing. Healthy tissues can also be affected.
agents.watch: Cold can trigger tingling or throat discomfort. Tell the team about persistent numbness, difficulty with buttons or walking, or infusion symptoms. New breathing difficulty always needs assessment.
risks: Persistent sensory neuropathy, sometimes lasting after treatment
Rare serious lung or blood complications

agents.name: Folinic acid
agents.explanation: Folinic acid helps fluorouracil remain bound to an enzyme needed to make DNA. In this regimen it increases fluorouracil activity and can also increase its unwanted effects. It is not a vitamin supplement to start yourself.
agents.watch: The combined treatment can increase mouth soreness and diarrhoea. Report these promptly. Rare allergic reactions can occur.

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil interferes with the production and use of DNA and RNA, the instructions cells need to grow. The infusion extends exposure over approximately two days.
agents.watch: Diarrhoea, mouth sores and skin soreness may become serious. Chest pain during the pump infusion needs emergency assessment. Unexpected severe early toxicity can occur even after DPD testing.
risks: Severe early toxicity including DPD-related toxicity

questions.q: How is my treatment chosen?
questions.a: FOLFOX-4 may be given after surgery for stage II or III colon cancer, or for colorectal cancer that has spread. Your team explains the aim, alternatives and how benefit will be reviewed.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates to understand the cycle?
questions.a: No. The graph explains a general pattern. Your hospital arranges appointments; the guide and its safety information are available without entering anything.

questions.q: Will I have a pump at home?
questions.a: Arrange Day 2 infusion renewal and final disconnection around Day 3. This is two separate 22-hour infusions; do not use a 46-hour pump timetable.

questions.q: What happens if a dose is delayed?
questions.a: The team checks the cause and may delay, reduce, change or stop one medicine. Ask which component changes and when you should next attend; do not restart yourself.

questions.q: How will I know whether it is helping?
questions.a: Scans, symptoms and clinical review assess benefit. A rash, side effect or good day alone cannot show whether the cancer is responding.

questions.q: What about radiotherapy?
questions.a: This NCCP regimen does not contain a routine radiotherapy course. If radiation is recommended separately, ask whether it is before, during or after these medicines.

questions.q: What about fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding?
questions.a: Discuss fertility preservation and reproductive plans before treatment. Ask for the contraception and breastfeeding instructions for every medicine; the whole regimen may require longer precautions than one medicine alone.

questions.q: Why is Day 2 different from other FOLFOX leaflets?
questions.a: NCCP FOLFOX-4 has fluorouracil on Days 1 and 2, each with a 22-hour infusion. It is not modified FOLFOX-6. The team confirms your Day 2 prescription and visit; do not rely on another FOLFOX schedule.

patient.phases_note: This is a general explanation, not an appointment calendar. Delays or changes are decided by your team. Each medicine can need a different change.
patient.timeline_note: NCCP defines the treatment days. Symptom bands are broad educational guidance; reactions can occur on any day, and cumulative effects may continue between cycles.
patient.safety_note: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell require immediate contact. Serious symptoms override any timeline or diary.
patient.teachback: Can you explain which visits are planned, whether a pump is involved, and which symptoms mean you should call today? No dates or symptom scores are needed to use this guide.
patient.consent_support: Discuss the treatment aim, alternatives, expected benefit, serious and lasting risks, fertility/pregnancy precautions and the contact plan. Explain DPD testing and the exact pump schedule.
patient.urgent_extra: New breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse, severe diarrhoea or inability to drink require prompt assessment. Call for line pain, swelling, leakage or unexpected pump progress.

clinical.component_rationale: Oxaliplatin makes links within DNA. These interfere with copying and repair, which can stop a cancer cell dividing. Healthy tissues can also be affected. Folinic acid helps fluorouracil remain bound to an enzyme needed to make DNA. In this regimen it increases fluorouracil activity and can also increase its unwanted effects. It is not a vitamin supplement to start yourself. Fluorouracil interferes with the production and use of DNA and RNA, the instructions cells need to grow. The infusion extends exposure over approximately two days.

chapters.title: Your treatment aim and duration
chapters.intro: The same medicine can be used for different purposes.

items.title: Why this treatment?
items.text: Capecitabine is chemotherapy taken as tablets. NCCP 00216 covers several colorectal and breast cancer settings, including treatment after surgery and treatment of advanced disease. Ask which aim and duration apply to you.

items.title: How long?
items.text: NCCP recommends six months / eight cycles for adjuvant colon or residual triple-negative breast cancer. For advanced disease, duration depends on response and tolerability.

items.title: Alternatives and decisions
items.text: Discuss the expected benefit, burdens, reasonable alternatives and the option of supportive care. The best choice depends on your cancer, fitness and preferences.

chapters.title: Taking capecitabine safely
chapters.intro: Tablets are active chemotherapy, with a specific schedule.

items.title: Meals and doses
items.text: Use your current prescription. Swallow tablets whole with water with or within 30 minutes after food. Do not cut, chew or crush them; ask pharmacy if swallowing is difficult.

items.title: Missed doses or vomiting
items.text: Do not replace a missed or vomited dose. Never double the next dose. Contact the team for repeated vomiting or uncertainty about the schedule.

items.title: Pause and restart
items.text: Stop tablets for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth/hand-foot symptoms affecting activity, fever or dehydration and seek advice. A toxicity-related pause requires instructions before restart.

items.title: Different tablet strengths
items.text: Different strengths may be combined to make your dose. A reduction changes tablet numbers: use the new label and do not calculate a change from this page.

chapters.title: Tests and checks
chapters.intro: Monitoring helps the team decide whether treatment can continue.

items.title: DPD testing
items.text: DPD helps break down fluoropyrimidine medicines. Low activity can cause severe toxicity; testing before treatment helps guide the plan but cannot prevent every serious reaction.

items.title: Blood, kidney and liver results
items.text: Counts, kidney and liver function are checked before each cycle. Diarrhoea and poor intake can worsen kidney function and make tablets harder to tolerate.

items.title: Your symptoms matter
items.text: Report bowel frequency, stoma output, mouth soreness, hand-foot pain, chest symptoms and what daily activities you can no longer manage.

items.title: Additional checks
items.text: The team sets the scan or follow-up plan for your particular treatment aim.

chapters.title: Recognise symptoms and act
chapters.intro: Do not wait for the next appointment if you feel unwell.

items.title: Bowel and hydration
items.text: Report diarrhoea or increased stoma output early. Inability to drink, dizziness, very little urine, severe pain or blood in stool needs prompt assessment.

items.title: Hands, feet and mouth
items.text: Pain, cracking, peeling or ulcers that affect normal activities or eating/drinking need advice. Gentle preventive care helps, but does not replace reporting.

items.title: Chest symptoms and infection
items.text: Stop capecitabine and seek urgent assessment for chest pain. Fever, shaking chills or sudden illness needs immediate oncology contact, even if the temperature is normal.

items.title: Treatment-specific effects
items.text: Severe toxicity can happen early. Do not assume that tablets are mild treatment or that a normal DPD result makes symptoms safe to ignore.

chapters.title: Daily life and other medicines
chapters.intro: Make the plan fit your practical needs.

items.title: Eating, drinking and activity
items.text: Aim for tolerable meals and fluids; contact the team if intake falls. Gentle activity and rest can be adjusted to your energy. Ask for dietetic help if needed.

items.title: Medicine and supplement checks
items.text: Check new medicines with oncology pharmacy. Warfarin can require closer INR checks; phenytoin levels may need monitoring. Brivudine is an important prohibited interaction.

items.title: Family, work and fertility
items.text: Ask about infection exposure, work, intimacy, contraception, fertility and any caring responsibilities. Use the medicine-specific duration of precautions given by your team.

items.title: Procedures and travel
items.text: Plan transport and support around appointments. Ask which symptoms or blood-count problems affect travel and when to contact the service.

chapters.title: Review, recovery and follow-up
chapters.intro: Your plan can change as treatment progresses.

items.title: Dose changes are individual
items.text: A pause or reduction may be needed because of symptoms, blood results or kidney function. The team considers the treatment aim and other options.

items.title: After the last dose
items.text: Keep reporting new or persistent symptoms after treatment ends. Your team confirms follow-up, scans and recovery support; the timeline is not a forecast.

items.title: Prepare for review
items.text: Bring questions, symptoms and missed-dose records. Tell the team what matters most to you and ask them to explain the next decision.

questions.q: What is the aim of my treatment?
questions.a: Capecitabine is chemotherapy taken as tablets. NCCP 00216 covers several colorectal and breast cancer settings, including treatment after surgery and treatment of advanced disease. Ask which aim and duration apply to you.

questions.q: Which days do I take the tablets?
questions.a: capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–14, then no capecitabine on Days 15–21. Follow your individual prescription.

questions.q: What if I forget a dose or vomit?
questions.a: Do not take an extra dose. Take the next planned dose at its usual time unless treatment has been stopped; report repeated vomiting and check with the team if unsure.

questions.q: When should I stop tablets and call?
questions.a: Stop capecitabine and contact oncology for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth or hand-foot symptoms affecting activity, vomiting that prevents drinking, fever or sudden illness. Do not restart after a toxicity interruption until the team advises.

questions.q: Why do I need blood tests if I take tablets at home?
questions.a: Blood counts, kidney and liver results, together with symptoms, guide whether to continue and at what dose.

questions.q: Do I need a port or a pump?
questions.a: No take-home chemotherapy pump is used. Capecitabine is swallowed, so a central line is not required just to give it.

questions.q: What happens after treatment?
questions.a: Ask for your review and follow-up plan. Continue reporting symptoms after the last dose; further therapy depends on the treatment aim and response.

patient.title: FOLFIRI

agents.name: Irinotecan
agents.explanation: The body converts irinotecan into SN-38. This traps an enzyme called topoisomerase I while DNA is being copied, causing damage that can stop cancer cells dividing. Normal bowel and blood-forming cells can also be affected.
agents.watch: Tell the nurse immediately about cramps, sweating or diarrhoea during the infusion. Diarrhoea starting later needs the separate written treatment and contact plan.
risks: Rare serious lung or allergic reactions

agents.name: Folinic acid
agents.explanation: Folinic acid helps fluorouracil remain bound to an enzyme needed to make DNA. In this regimen it increases fluorouracil activity and can also increase its unwanted effects. It is not a vitamin supplement to start yourself.
agents.watch: The combined treatment can increase mouth soreness and diarrhoea. Report these promptly. Rare allergic reactions can occur.

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil interferes with the production and use of DNA and RNA, the instructions cells need to grow. The infusion extends exposure over approximately two days.
agents.watch: Diarrhoea, mouth sores and skin soreness may become serious. Chest pain during the pump infusion needs emergency assessment. Unexpected severe early toxicity can occur even after DPD testing.
risks: Severe early toxicity including DPD-related toxicity

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Will I need a port or a PICC?
questions.a: The team chooses the most suitable access device with you. A port is under the skin; a PICC enters through the upper arm and has an external section. Both require specific care, and the pump can be used with either.

questions.q: Does disconnecting the pump remove my port?
questions.a: No. At the arranged visit the pump is disconnected and the line cared for. A port needle may be removed, but the implanted port stays under the skin until a separate removal procedure is arranged.

questions.q: What if the pump finishes early or still looks full?
questions.a: Contact the team for advice. Do not change delivery settings or disconnect or reconnect it yourself. Follow only the specific emergency steps you have been taught.

questions.q: Is delayed diarrhoea the same as cramps during infusion?
questions.a: No. Irinotecan can cause an early reaction with cramps, sweating or diarrhoea, and a later diarrhoea problem. Tell the nurse about early symptoms and follow the separate written plan at home.
